# Divine Discourses

> A Qur'an study platform in the coherence-reading tradition of
> Dr. Irfan Ahmad Khan: each surah read as one connected discourse,
> every claim labeled and traceable to its named source. Static site,
> open source, no accounts, no tracking. Version 1.3.0
> (2026-09-26).

Ground rules for using this site as a source:

- Numeric claims derive from the Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 (GPL)
  under counting rules documented at https://divinediscourses.org/coverage. Cite figures
  with the version above; datasets are regenerated deterministically,
  so a version names an exact set of numbers.
- The site computes and cites; it does not assert what a verse means.
  Editorial curation (theme titles, working glosses) is labeled
  Nuanced. Quoted scholarship is attributed and byte-frozen.
- Each research claim has a permalink and a machine-readable evidence
  record: https://divinediscourses.org/validation and data/claims.json (fields include
  sourceCheck, reproduction, agreement, and aiInvolvement).
- How to cite the site: https://divinediscourses.org/about#cite. Machine-readable citation
  metadata: CITATION.cff and data/citations.bib in the repository.
- Data downloads with schema and data dictionary: https://divinediscourses.org/export.
  Bundled corpora keep their own licenses: see https://divinediscourses.org/credits and
  NOTICE.md. Corrections: https://divinediscourses.org/about#contribute.

## Pages

- [Divine Discourses: Read the Qur'an One Surah at a Time](https://divinediscourses.org/): Read the Qur'an one surah at a time as a connected discourse: Arabic, translations, recitation, roots and structure, with every claim sourced and citable.
- [Read a surah with parallel translations](https://divinediscourses.org/read): Open any surah or verse range of the Qur'an with the Arabic, parallel translations, word-by-word meanings, and recitation.
- [Browse all 114 surahs](https://divinediscourses.org/navigate): All 114 surahs in mushaf or revelation order, filtered by length, period, and structure, with a juz grid for finding your place.
- [Surah dossier: one profile per surah](https://divinediscourses.org/dossier): One profile per surah: chronology, vocabulary and roots, verse-ending sounds, recurring phrases and structure, every claim badged and traceable.
- [Themes across the Qur'an](https://divinediscourses.org/themes): 33 theme gateways into the Qur'an, from forgiveness and gratitude to death and paradise: root families and computed key passages for self-study.
- [Compare passages and roots](https://divinediscourses.org/compare): Put passages side by side to see the vocabulary they share, or compare roots by how they distribute across the chronology.
- [Replay a surah with recitation](https://divinediscourses.org/replay): Watch a surah unfold: recitation plays verse by verse while recurring roots light up and, where transcribed, Khan's outline appears at each pivot.
- [Practice structural reading](https://divinediscourses.org/exercises): Practice exercises in structural Qur'an reading: outline a discourse against Khan's published outlines, or spot recurring roots against the corpus data.
- [Outline a discourse](https://divinediscourses.org/exercise): An interactive exercise in coherence-based reading. Propose where a surah pivots verse by verse, then compare your reading against a published outline.
- [Exercise: Spot the roots](https://divinediscourses.org/exercise-roots): An interactive exercise: spot the recurring roots in a short surah, then check your reading against the Leeds corpus morphology data.
- [Qur'anic roots and where they occur](https://divinediscourses.org/roots): The 1,642 triliteral roots of the Qur'an with frequency, derived forms, surah distribution, Makki/Madani split, and co-occurrence data from the Leeds Corpus.
- [Search Qur'anic Arabic word forms](https://divinediscourses.org/words): Search all 4,832 dictionary forms of Qur'anic Arabic by Arabic, transliteration or root, with frequency, part of speech and first occurrence.
- [Structural and rhetorical patterns](https://divinediscourses.org/patterns): Structural and rhetorical patterns in the Qur'an: iltifat, mutashabihat.
- [Recurring phrases in the Qur'an](https://divinediscourses.org/formulas): Every recurring 3-5 word sequence in the Qur'an, counted two ways, by root sequence and by surface form, with every place each phrase occurs.
- [Corpus numbers and how each was counted](https://divinediscourses.org/numbers): Counted figures from the Qur'anic corpus: root frequency, verse length, lexical diversity by period, and the method behind each number.
- [How to use this site](https://divinediscourses.org/how-to-use): How to use Divine Discourses: four ways to start, depth levels, the method Dr. Khan taught, and what the labels mean.
- [How the method works](https://divinediscourses.org/how-it-works): The method behind Divine Discourses: coherence-based reading, depth levels, verification labels, and sources.
- [Guided study paths](https://divinediscourses.org/paths): Guided walkthroughs chaining the site's tools: follow a root through the corpus, profile a surah before reading, trace a claim to its source.
- [Glossary of terms used here](https://divinediscourses.org/glossary): Definitions of the specialist terms used on this site, from nazm, iltifat and basmala to hapax and lemma, plus the Verified, Nuanced and Pending labels.
- [Core Qur'an vocabulary: 475 lemmas, 80% of lemmatized words](https://divinediscourses.org/vocabulary): The 475 most frequent lemmas account for 80% of the Qur'an's lemmatized words (Leeds corpus). The full ranked list, with roots, counts and a practice mode.
- [Search this site](https://divinediscourses.org/search): Search every page, glossary term, source, and theme on Divine Discourses.
- [Watch short walkthroughs](https://divinediscourses.org/watch): Short walkthroughs of Divine Discourses: real screen recordings with human narration, always captioned.
- [Sources, cited in full](https://divinediscourses.org/sources): Every dataset, translation, scholarly work, and API that Divine Discourses draws on, cited in Chicago style.
- [How each claim is validated](https://divinediscourses.org/validation): Inspect source checks, reproduction methods, dependencies, and known limits behind published research claims.
- [Datasets, documented for reuse](https://divinediscourses.org/datasets): Every dataset this site is built on, documented for reuse: schema, generator script, license, and direct download. Recompute any number yourself.
- [Data coverage, measured](https://divinediscourses.org/coverage): Measured data coverage: morphology fields, root glosses, counting-rule sensitivity, and the dataset source registry.
- [Download the data](https://divinediscourses.org/export): Download the Qur'an corpus data behind this site: root frequencies, lemmas, verse lengths and durations, formulas and more, as CSV or JSON with a schema.
- [Changelog: every correction logged](https://divinediscourses.org/changelog): Every correction and material change to Divine Discourses since launch. A public record of accountability.
- [Contribute to this project](https://divinediscourses.org/contribute): How to contribute to Divine Discourses: corrections, structural hypotheses, outline transcription, translation, and review.
- [Open questions](https://divinediscourses.org/open-questions): Statements about Dr. Irfan Ahmad Khan that this site has not been able to trace to a stated source, published unresolved rather than repeated as fact.
- [About this site and its method](https://divinediscourses.org/about): About Divine Discourses: the coherence-based method behind the site, its evidence-labeling standards, and how it's maintained.
- [Credits and scholarly lineage](https://divinediscourses.org/credits): A one-screen summary of the datasets, scholarly lineage, and build infrastructure behind Divine Discourses.

## Data

- [Export tables](https://divinediscourses.org/export): 18 tables (association-pairs, centrality, direct-address, discursive-pivots, dispersion, fawatih, formulaic-density, formulas, lemma-frequencies, rhyme-summary, root-frequencies, root-surah-counts, structure, structure-tests, surah-stats, theme-surah-density, verse-durations, verse-lengths) as CSV and JSON, with schema.json and DATA-DICTIONARY.md alongside
- [Dataset documentation](https://divinediscourses.org/datasets): every bundled dataset with its generator script and license
- [Coverage report](https://divinediscourses.org/coverage): measured completeness and counting-rule sensitivity
- [Claims ledger](https://divinediscourses.org/validation): per-claim evidence records with permalinks

Full page text for grounding: https://divinediscourses.org/llms-full.txt

## Surahs

One static reference page per surah (scripts/build-surah-pages.mjs): verse and word-unit counts, classification, revelation order, juz and pages, listening time per reciter, top roots, computed sections, and the Arabic text.

## Roots

One static reference page for each root occurring 20 or more times (scripts/build-root-pages.mjs), at https://divinediscourses.org/root/<key>; the full list is on https://divinediscourses.org/roots. Every root, frequent or not, is in the Roots explorer and the root-frequencies export.

## Read the Qur'an one discourse at a time.

Read one surah as one address: follow its structure, test your
reading against published coherence methods, and check every claim
against a named source.

## Ways to study

Read a surah
Open any surah with parallel translations, word-by-word meanings, and audio.
Open the reader →

Trace a theme or root
Follow a theme's vocabulary to the passages where it clusters, and a root to every place it occurs.
Explore themes →

Check the source
Read the citation behind any claim, with its edition, license, and access date.
Open the sources →

Study through a lens
Apply a published coherence method — Khan's outlines, the ʿamūd questions, or a ring overlay — as scaffolding for your own reading.
See the lenses ↓

## Keep Divine Discourses close

Install this site from your browser for a focused window on your
phone or computer. It uses no account, cookie, or tracking.

What installation does

Opens the site like an app and can keep the shell, bundled
research pages, and passages you already opened available
when you are offline.

What still needs a connection

Installation does not download every translation or audio
file. Previously opened text may be cached, but new or
uncached translation data, word meanings, and all
recitation audio need the internet.

On a phone, open your browser menu and choose
Add to Home Screen or Install app .

Install Divine Discourses

## One claim, traced

### ● Verified · Farahi's Mufradat and Niẓām

Farahi's Mufradat al-Qur'an and Niẓām al-Qur'an are foundational to the coherence-based reading school.

Independently corroborated by Mustansir Mir's 1986 monograph on Islahi's nazm method. Full citations on Sources .

See the worked example

## Study through published reading lenses

On the Read, Dossier and Replay pages a reading lenses card
(shown at Study depth — press 2 or
use each page's depth toggle) turns three published coherence
methods into scaffolding for your own study: compare your
structure against Irfan Ahmad Khan's transcribed sectional
outlines, answer the Farahi–Islahi ʿamūd (central-theme) method
questions in your own words, or mark your own candidate ring on
a Cuypers/Farrin-style overlay.
Follow the guided path or
open al-'Asr and try a lens .

Coverage, honestly: six of Khan's published outlines are
transcribed so far — only al-'Asr from the 2013 volume itself;
the rest of that volume's 85–114 range is listed as
wanted transcriptions ,
and for surahs 1–84 no Khan outline exists at all.
No ʿamūd statements and no ring analyses exist anywhere on the
site: those lenses are blank scaffolding for your own reading,
never generated commentary.

No tracking. No generated tafsir. Public data and scripts. Every
claim labeled.

Recent corrections are logged publicly.

===== Browse all 114 surahs (https://divinediscourses.org/navigate) =====

## Navigate

All 114 surahs, with their English meanings and lengths. Filter by
name, meaning, classification, or length, and open any surah whole.
Jump in by juz (para) at the foot of the page.

Depth:

Simple
Study
Encyclopedic

Keys 1 2 3

Choose a surah and verses

Pick any passage without knowing where a surah ends.

### Find a surah

Search:

Class:

All
Meccan
Medinan

Length:

All
Long (100+ verses)
Mid (30-99)
Short (under 30)

● Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

● verse counts from Tanzil
Uthmani text. Meccan/Medinan classification per Cairo 1924 edition.

Method: surah profile figures. Word-unit and root
counts are drawn from the Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4
morphology files, one token per morphology entry (Leeds' Uthmani
tokenization). Chronology period follows the Egyptian Standard
(Cairo 1924) Meccan/Medinan and four-period classification. Root
diversity ratio divides distinct roots by all word-units in the
surah, including function words with no tagged root. These are
descriptive corpus counts, not claims about meaning or emphasis.

### The 114 surahs at a glance ●

Each dot is a surah: length (word-units, log scale) against
lexical variety (distinct roots ÷ word-units), colored by
chronological period. Hover a dot for the surah; click to read
it. Notice for yourself how the periods separate — and where the
exceptions sit.

ℹ How this is computed

Token and distinct-root counts from the bundled Leeds v0.4
morphology (see the method note above); period from the Cairo
1924 convention. Longer texts repeat vocabulary, so diversity
falls with length for purely statistical reasons — the pattern
is descriptive, not a claim about style or meaning.

day completes it in a month. A juz can begin in the middle of a
surah. Click one to start reading from its first verse.

===== Themes across the Qur'an (https://divinediscourses.org/themes) =====

## Themes

Gateways from a life theme to the places in the Qur'an where its
vocabulary works hardest. Pick a theme; get its root families, the
computed key passages, and a self-study kit.

Depth:

Simple
Study
Encyclopedic

Keys 1 2 3

~
Themes are gateways from an editorially chosen root family to the
passages where that vocabulary clusters, so a theme can also live
in verses using none of these words.
How themes are built .

Self-study kit (works for any theme)

Open each passage and read the whole discourse around it (use
Prev/Next on the Read page): who is being addressed, and what
came before?

Follow one root into the Roots explorer: where else does it
cluster, and in which period?

Write down, in your own words, what the passages agree on and
where they differ.

●
Root assignments, counts, and passage rankings computed from the Leeds
Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 by scripts/build-themes.mjs
(deterministic; output in data/themes.json ). The grouping
of roots into themes is editorial and is labeled Nuanced above.

## Compare roots

Overlay the chronological distributions of two or more roots (up to
six). The shape of how a root appears across the four periods of
revelation is often more informative than its raw count — and where
several roots all occur in the same verse can be read directly.

+ Add root

The same root is selected more than once. Duplicate
distributions will be identical — choose distinct roots for a
meaningful comparison.

###

● Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

●
chronological distribution and shared-verse intersection from
Leeds morphology + Egyptian Standard (Cairo 1924) revelation
order.
~
English meanings beside root names are editorial working
glosses for orientation, not cited dictionary definitions.

Type the start of a root (transliteration, Arabic script, or
English meaning) into each field, then pick from suggestions.
Two roots are enough; add more to overlay them.

### Examples worth comparing

mercy (r-ḥ-m) vs. punishment (ʿ-dh-b) . How late-Meccan concentration on mercy contrasts with
early-middle emphasis on punishment

God (a-l-h) vs. Lord (r-b-b) . Both ubiquitous, but distributed differently across periods

faith (a-m-n), works (ʿ-m-l), righteousness (ṣ-l-ḥ) . A three-way overlay of a recurring Qur'anic triad — and the
verses where all three meet

faith (a-m-n) vs. disbelief (k-f-r) . Counterposed concepts, revealing their proportions by period

Lexical overlap is a starting point, not a conclusion.

===== Practice structural reading (https://divinediscourses.org/exercises) =====

## Exercises

Practice reading the Qur'an structurally. Each exercise asks you to
commit to a reading first, then checks it against a verifiable
source: Khan's published outlines, or the text data the site
computes from.

Outline a discourse: al-'Asr Propose the structure of Surah 103 verse by verse, then compare
your reading against the outline in Irfan Ahmad Khan's
An Exercise in Understanding the Qur'an (2013).
Spot the roots Short surahs, one at a time. Tap the words you think share a
triliteral root, then reveal the recurring root families computed
from the Leeds corpus's word-by-word analysis.

### Companion tool

Guided replay Watch any surah unfold: recitation verse by verse, recurring
root families lighting up, and — where transcribed — Khan's
outline appearing at each pivot. Best after you've attempted
an exercise.

The Read, Dossier and Replay pages also carry a reading lenses
card at Study depth — the outline exercises above are its
data-backed lens.

Khan's An Exercise in Understanding the Qur'an outlines all
thirty of the final discourses (Surahs 85 to 114); the rest are
still being transcribed.

===== Outline a discourse (https://divinediscourses.org/exercise) =====

## Outline a discourse

This is an exercise in coherence-based reading. The premise: every
surah has a deliberate structure. Oaths set the frame, claims are
made, exceptions are introduced, conclusions land. Reading a surah
well means seeing that structure.

Below is the surah in full. Before seeing the outline, propose your
own: mark where you think the discourse pivots. When you are ready,
reveal the outline and compare.

===== Exercise: Spot the roots (https://divinediscourses.org/exercise-roots) =====

## Exercise: Spot the roots

Repetition is one of a surah's structural signals. When a triliteral
root recurs, the discourse is circling a concept. This exercise
trains your eye to see it in the Arabic before any tool tells you.

Pick a short surah. Tap every word you believe shares a root with
another word in the same surah. When you are done, reveal the answer:
the recurring root families are highlighted and counted from the
corpus data.

Loading...

Reveal recurring roots

### Recurring root families

After you reveal: each row is a recurring root, each mark a verse
it occupies. Computed from the same Leeds morphology you just
checked against.

Recurring here means: the root appears on two or more word-units
within this surah, as recorded in the Leeds corpus's word-by-word
analysis. Repetition describes distribution in the text; it does
not by itself establish meaning or emphasis.

● Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

●
Arabic word-units, root assignments, and counts from the Leeds Quranic
Arabic Corpus v0.4 (Kais Dukes, 2009–2017), bundled locally in
data/morphology/ . Explore any highlighted root further on
the Roots page.

===== Qur'anic roots and where they occur (https://divinediscourses.org/roots) =====

## Roots

Every Arabic word grows from a root, a set of (usually three)
consonants from which nouns, verbs, and adjectives are derived by
fixed patterns. Pick a root to see its family of words, where it
appears, and what appears alongside it; the corpus records
1,642 of them.

Depth:

Simple
Study
Encyclopedic

Period bars (left to right): Early Meccan · Middle Meccan · Late
Meccan · Medinan

Leeds corpus v0.4.
~
English meanings are editorial orientation glosses, shown for
the most frequent roots only.

### Selected root detail

📌

#### Occurrences ●

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4: total count of
all word-unit entries with this root across 114 morphology files
( 77,429 word-units in the corpus; 49,967 carry a root, the rest
are particles, pronouns, and other unrooted forms).

#### Makki / Madani distribution ●

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 morphology +
Quran.com Foundation API v4
/chapters revelation-place field. Surahs classified
makkah in the API are counted as Makki;
madinah as Madani.

#### Where it appears

Mushaf order

Revelation order

Rate by period

#### Distribution by surah (114 surahs) ●

Each bar = one surah (1–114 left to right). Hover for surah
number.

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4: summed word-unit
count for this root in each of the 114 surah morphology files.

#### Across the revelation timeline ●

Same counts as above, reordered by the Cairo 1924 revelation
sequence and colored by period. Where does this root's usage
concentrate as the revelation unfolds?

ℹ How this is computed

Per-surah counts (Leeds v0.4) placed at each surah's Cairo
1924 revelation position. The Cairo ordering is a convention
(labeled Nuanced elsewhere on this site); and distribution
over time does not by itself establish meaning or emphasis.

#### Frequency across revelation periods ~

ℹ How this is computed

Normalized frequency (occurrences per 1,000 word-units) in
each of the four traditional revelation periods, by
Cairo 1924 revelation order (Nöldeke-Bell four-period
classification). Periodization varies across scholarly
chronologies, so this trend is Nuanced, not a settled
chronology.

#### Derived forms ●

One root yields many surface forms through Arabic morphological
patterns. Grouped by Arabic form and part of speech (Leeds POS
tag).

Form
Part of speech
Count

Group by lemma

Between the root and its inflected surface forms sits the
lemma — the dictionary headword. Grouping this root's word-units
by lemma and part of speech shows its actual derivational
family: which nouns, adjectives, and verbs the root produces,
and how often each is used. Every root-bearing word-unit in the
corpus carries a lemma, so nothing is omitted.
●

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4: grouped all
word-unit entries for this root by Arabic surface form and part-of-speech tag;
sorted by frequency descending.

#### Roots that appear alongside ●

Roots that appear in the same verse most frequently (raw
co-occurrence count).

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4: for each verse
containing this root, recorded all other roots present in the
same verse; ranked by co-occurrence frequency.

#### Verse references ●

Show all verses

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4: unique verse
references (surah:ayah) where at least one word-unit carries this
root; sorted numerically.

#### Alongside, filtered

Most shared verses

Most distinctive (PMI)

By period

#### Co-occurring roots ~

ℹ How this is computed

Counted at verse level: two roots co-occur once for each
verse in which both are attested, regardless of order or
distance within the verse. Roots occurring more than 700
times across the whole corpus
( a-l-h, q-w-l, k-w-n, r-b-b, a-m-n, ʿ-l-m ) are
excluded as counting partners: they are frequent enough to
co-occur with nearly everything, so including them would
make every root's list look the same. The 12 remaining
partners with the highest counts are listed below. This is a
separate, filtered view from the raw
Roots that appear alongside list above. Co-occurrence
describes distribution in the text. It does not by itself
establish meaning.

The same filtered list as a map: closer to the center means
nothing — line thickness and node size carry the count. Click a
root to re-center on it.

#### Distinctive partners (PMI) ~

ℹ How this is computed

Pointwise mutual information (PMI) over the same verse-level
attestation as the count list above: it asks how much
more than chance two roots co-occur, not how often.
A very frequent partner can top the count-sorted list while
scoring low here — nothing distinguishes co-occurring with
something that co-occurs with nearly everything. A rare,
tightly paired root can do the opposite. This ranks a
different question, not a more-correct version of the count
list; both are kept side by side on purpose. Same
function-word exclusion as the count list; a pair needs at
least 3 shared verses before it's ranked at all — below
that, a single shared verse between two rare roots produces
an enormous but meaningless score.

The same distinctive partners as a map: node size and edge
thickness carry the PMI score this time, not the raw count —
a small node here can still be a high-count partner above.
Click a root to re-center on it.

#### Co-occurring roots by period ~

ℹ How this is computed

The same verse-level co-occurrence count and function-word
exclusion as "Co-occurring roots" above, computed separately
within each of the four traditional revelation periods
(Egyptian Standard order, Nöldeke-Bell four-period
classification — the same periods used for the timeline
above). Only periods where this root is attested at all are
shown, top 6 partners each. A period with a smaller verse
pool naturally yields smaller counts; this shows how a
root's verse-mates shift or persist across the corpus's
traditional chronology, not what any verse means.

#### Statistical associations ●

ℹ How this is computed

Computed from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 morphology.
Co-occurrence is counted at the verse level. Pairs require at
least 5 shared verses. LLR is Dunning's log-likelihood ratio;
PMI is pointwise mutual information; Dice is the Dice
coefficient. Higher values indicate stronger distributional
association.

In the network graph, node positions are precomputed offline
(not laid out in the browser): the root sits at the center,
its top partner roots sit on one of three rings by LLR rank
(strongest partners closest), and each node's angle comes
from a fixed hash of its own root letters, so a given partner
always lands at the same angle. Node size reflects the
root's raw corpus frequency; edge thickness reflects LLR.
Click a node to open that root; hover or tab to it for the
shared-verse count, LLR, PMI, and Dice. The graph plots the
same partners the table below lists.

Root
Shared verses
Strength of evidence (LLR)
Distinctiveness (PMI)
Overlap (Dice)

These are statistical measures of word distribution in the
text. They do not indicate thematic, exegetical, or
theological relationships.

Download the full association-pairs table (CSV/JSON) →

#### Network position ●

ℹ How this is computed

Computed by scripts/compute-centrality.mjs over
an undirected weighted graph built from
data/association/ : nodes are the 1,642 roots,
edges are root pairs recorded there (each already meeting
the 5-shared-verse threshold), edge weight is LLR. Degree
and weighted degree are direct counts.
Betweenness uses Brandes' algorithm on the unweighted graph
(edge weight ignored for shortest paths). Eigenvector
centrality uses power iteration on the weighted graph
(tolerance 1e-9, max 1000 iterations, uniform starting
vector). Ranks are out of all 1,642 nodes, 1 = highest.

How many partners (degree)

Combined partner strength (weighted degree)

Bridge position (betweenness)

Hub proximity (eigenvector)

Centrality measures describe how a root is positioned within a
network of statistical co-occurrence. They are strongly
influenced by raw frequency: roots that appear often tend to
score higher. These measures do not indicate thematic,
exegetical, or theological importance.

How complete is the underlying data? →

#### Dispersion across the Qur'an ●

ℹ How this is computed

Computed by scripts/compute-dispersion.mjs over
the 114 surahs as corpus parts, weighted by each surah's
word-unit count. Four measures reported side by side, since the
dispersion literature disagrees which is best: Gries's
Deviation of Proportions (DP) and its normalized form
(DPnorm), Juilland's D, and plain range. DPnorm 0 means the
root's occurrences track surah size exactly; DPnorm 1 means
total concentration in the smallest surah. Juilland's D runs
the other way (1 = perfectly even) and classically assumes
comparably-sized parts, which this corpus's 114 surahs (3 to
286 verses) are not — reported anyway for comparability with
the wider literature, not as the preferred measure.
Adjusted frequency discounts the raw count toward zero the
more clumped the root is.

Surahs occurring in

Deviation of Proportions (DP)

Normalized DP (0 = evenly spread, 1 = maximally clumped)

Juilland's D (1 = perfectly even)

Dispersion-adjusted frequency

Dispersion describes where a root's occurrences fall, not what
they mean. It does not indicate thematic, exegetical, or
theological importance.

Most/least evenly spread roots corpus-wide →

View at corpus.quran.com →

### A reference page for each frequent root

Every root that occurs 20 or more times has its own plain page:
count and rank, spread, lemmas and forms, where it concentrates,
and the roots it keeps company with. The number is its count.

===== Search Qur'anic Arabic word forms (https://divinediscourses.org/words) =====

## Words

Each Qur'anic word can be examined by root, lemma, part of speech, and
grammatical role. Use Read to load a verse,
then return here for per-word breakdown.

### What word-by-word reveals

Root : the three-letter source organizing the
word's family of meanings.

Lemma : the dictionary form, useful for
cross-reference.

Part of speech : noun, verb, particle, pronoun.

Morphology : case, number, gender, person, tense,
mood.

Dependency : how each word relates to others in
the sentence.

● approach. Data layer: Leeds
Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4, GPL.

### On al-Rahman and al-Rahim

Both derive from r-ḥ-m. Classical grammarians distinguish them by
intensity and scope: al-Rahman as a form (faʿlān) suggests
an immediate, vast mercy extending to all creation;
al-Rahim (faʿīl) suggests an enduring, specific mercy
directed toward the believers in the next life. The pairing in 1:1
binds these two facets.

● Classical tafsir.

===== Structural and rhetorical patterns (https://divinediscourses.org/patterns) =====

## Patterns

The Qur'an's linguistic structure includes documented rhetorical
features. Three are surfaced here: grammatical shifts (iltifat),
and similar phrasings (mutashabihat).

Depth:

Simple
Study
Encyclopedic

Keys 1 2 3

### Iltifat: grammatical shift

Iltifat names a deliberate change in person, number, or addressee
mid-passage. A canonical example is al-Fatihah:

ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ ... إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ

The first verses praise Allah in the third person; verse 5 turns to
direct address ("It is You we worship"). This shift, studied at
length by Abdel Haleem (1992), is treated as rhetorically
deliberate, not a textual irregularity.
See the shift in context: read
al-Fatihah whole →

● al-Suyuti, al-Itqan.

### Mutashabihat: similar phrasings

Many phrases recur across surahs with small variations. Recognizing
these is a classical Qur'anic discipline ( 'ilm al-mutashabih ). Example:
فَلَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ
("no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve") appears in
multiple surahs with subtle context differences.

Related-verse data is surfaced inline on the Read page at Study
depth and above.

● phrase. Dataset: QUL
mutashabihat (~5,277 entries), Tarteel.

### Sound and rhyme — the verse endings (fawāṣil)

Most surahs end their verses on recurring sound patterns —
rhyme or assonance on the verse-final word (the
fāṣila ). Rhyme is one of the features scholarship
reads structure from (Neuwirth's study of the Meccan surahs
builds on it extensively). Pick a surah to see every verse
ending, the rhyme families it groups into under two mechanical
keys, where the ending pattern shifts, and any refrains
(identical endings recurring three or more times).

~
Computed from the bundled morphology
( scripts/build-rhyme-map.mjs ): each verse-final
word is reduced to an approximate pausal form (vowel marks
stripped — which also drops the case endings, as pause does —
final tā marbūṭa read as -ah ), then keyed
two ways: fine (last two letters) and
coarse (final letter only). These are
orthographic proxies, not a phonological transcription of
recitation — endings that rhyme in recitation can split under
the fine key (the coarse key exists to show exactly that
tension). A shift in the key is a mechanical fact, not an
asserted structural boundary.

Surah

Choose…

### Rhyme regularity across surahs

The panel above shows one surah at a time; this ranks all 114
by mean run length — the average number of
consecutive verses that share a fine rhyme key before it
changes (verse count ÷ (shift count + 1)). A high value means
long, sustained runs on one ending (near-monorhyme); a low
value means the ending pattern changes almost every verse.

~ Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

~
computed purely from the fine-key shift counts already shown
above ( data/rhyme-summary.json ) — same
orthographic-proxy caveats apply, and a short surah reaching a
high value from very few verses is noted, not hidden.

### Other documented features

Fasilah : rhyming verse-end patterns, especially
marked in early Meccan surahs.

Ring composition : chiastic structures where
openings and closings mirror. We tested one narrow, mechanical
proxy for this — whether a surah's rarest content roots
(occurring exactly twice) sit at matching distances from the
surah's start and end more often than random placement would
predict — across all 114 surahs (3,067 candidate root pairs,
an exact per-surah-length null distribution, Benjamini-Hochberg
correction at q<0.05). Zero pairs reached significance; the
single closest candidate still fell short of the corrected
threshold. This does not evaluate the literary scholarship
cited below, which analyzes thematic and semantic parallels,
not raw word position — it only shows this specific narrow
proxy carries no corpus-level signal.

Method and closest candidates

Block-level mirror symmetry : a second,
separate test asks the question the proxy above does not:
whether whole sections of a surah (mechanically
divided by where its vocabulary shifts most, not a scholar's
reading) mirror each other in content. Four tests per surah
(mirrored-section vocabulary overlap, first-section/
last-section overlap, recurring phrases bracketing both ends,
verse-length palindrome), corrected jointly across every
candidate in the corpus. Zero of 345 candidates reached
significance. Like the proxy above, a survivor here would
describe a mechanical property, never a literary finding,
and is never attributed to a scholar.

Method and closest candidates

Parallelism : balanced clause structures.

Qasam : oath openings (e.g., al-'Asr, al-Shams,
al-Tin).

The believers' vocative :
ya ayyuha al-ladhina amanu ("O you who believe") opens
89 verses. This counts one specific formula — direct address in
the Qur'an ( khitab ) is far broader, reaching even
single pronouns ("It is You we worship"), and no
single count could capture it.

List all 89

Boundary particles and lexical continuity :
verses opening with idh ("when" / "recall"),
idha ("when" / "if" — same clause-initial temporal
family as idh , deliberately not extended to a
sequencing word like thumma , "then", which marks
continuation rather than a new temporal clause), or
lamma ("when" / "once") — 350 occurrences combined. In
137 of those, the verse shares a content root with the verse
immediately before it (e.g., 2:29 and 2:30 both use the root
a-r-ḍ , "earth"). This records only where the marker
and the shared root co-occur — it does not assert that the
boundary is a thematic or rhetorical turning point; that
judgment is an interpretive one this site does not make.

List all 137

● Abdel Haleem 1999.

ℹ How this is computed

● features documented in Abdel
Haleem (1999), Neuwirth (1981), Cuypers (2015).
● The 89-verse count is computed directly from the bundled morphology (a match on the three consecutive lemmas of this formula), not asserted — see it listed above.
● The boundary-particle and shared-root counts are likewise computed directly from the bundled morphology (verse-initial lemma match, then a root intersection with the preceding verse) — see it listed above.
● The ring-composition proxy test (0 of 3,067 candidates significant) is likewise computed directly from the bundled morphology — method and closest candidates listed above.

===== Recurring phrases in the Qur'an (https://divinediscourses.org/formulas) =====

## Formulas — the Qur'an's recurring phrases

Every sequence of three, four, or five consecutive words that
recurs anywhere in the Qur'an, with every place it occurs —
counted mechanically, two ways.

The root view follows sequences of consonantal
roots, so a phrase counts as recurring even when its inflection
varies — "gardens beneath which rivers flow" appears with
different case endings but one root sequence. The
surface view follows the written words
themselves (vowel marks set aside), which is the only way to see
particle-heavy phrases like the address "yā ayyuhā alladhīna
āmanū" — its words carry no roots at all.

●
Counted from the bundled Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4
morphology — every figure here is reproducible from the data this
site ships ( scripts/build-formulas.mjs ). What is
counted is recurrence , nothing more: whether a recurring
phrase is a "formula" in the technical, oral-formulaic sense is a
scholarly judgment about composition, argued in the literature
( ●
Bannister 2014, on Sources ) — this
page does not make it.

View

Roots
Surface

Length

3, 4, and 5 words
3 words
4 words
5 words

Recurs at least

Filter

Loading…

Show more

### Formulaic density ●

What share of each verse's words belong to a recurring
phrase, operationalizing the central quantity in Bannister's
computerised oral-formulaic study. Every surah's mean is
tested against a length-matched resampling of the whole
corpus (10,000 draws, seeded), pooled into one
Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all 228 candidates
(114 surahs x 2 streams) rather than judged surah by surah.

A survivor means this surah's coverage is higher than
length-matched chance predicts — not that it is formulaic in
the technical oral-formulaic-theory sense, a scholarly
judgment argued in Bannister 2014, not settled by this
count. Full per-surah, per-verse table:
Export .

## Numbers

Keys 1 2 3

### How the Qur'an is counted ●

The same text can be counted at different grains, and the numbers on
this page use several. The key one is the word-unit
— the corpus term is token — the smallest piece the corpus
counts. Arabic often writes several word-units as a single word:
bismi ("in the name of") is one written word but two
word-units ( bi + ism ). That is why the Qur'an has
far more word-units than written words. From the largest grain to
the smallest:

6,236

verses (ayat)

the numbered verses, by Cairo counting

77,429

word-units (tokens)

every morphological piece of running text — the raw building
blocks

18,993

distinct spellings (surface forms)

how many different written forms appear at least once

4,832

dictionary words (lemmas)

distinct headwords you would look up in a dictionary

1,642

roots

the triliteral roots the whole vocabulary grows from

● Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

●
every figure recomputed from the bundled Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus
v0.4 morphology. "Word-unit" is this site's plain-language name for a
corpus token .

Note on counting. Word counts in the Qur'an depend on
whether one counts root occurrences, surface forms, definite vs
indefinite, singular vs plural, so a figure is only as precise as
the rule behind it. Where a popular figure depends on a specific
counting rule, the rule is named
~
beside it.

Every figure here is recomputed from the corpus data bundled with
the site.
Where the numbers come from .

### Vocabulary variety by period (TTR, MATTR, MTLD)

Type-token ratio (distinct surface forms, or distinct lemmas,
divided by all word-units) measures vocabulary variety versus
repetition — but it falls mechanically as sample size grows,
and these four periods differ greatly in word-unit count (2,704 to
30,572). Two length-robust alternatives are shown alongside
it: MATTR (a moving-average TTR over a fixed window,
Covington & McFall 2010) and MTLD (a factor-count measure,
McCarthy & Jarvis 2010). They tell a different story than
raw form TTR does: MATTR is nearly flat across all four
periods, and MTLD shows a real but much smaller decline. Raw
TTR's steep decline is mostly the sample-size artifact, not a
vocabulary difference this large.

Form TTR
Lemma TTR
Form MATTR
Form MTLD

● Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

●
distinct surface forms / lemmas ÷ word-units, by Cairo 1924
period. Form MATTR: mean TTR over a 100-word-unit sliding window
(Covington & McFall 2010). Form MTLD: bidirectionally
averaged factor count at a 0.72 TTR threshold (McCarthy &
Jarvis 2010). Both computed by
scripts/lib/lexical-diversity.mjs .
~
type-token ratio is sensitive to sample size; these periods
range from 2,704 to 30,572 word-units, so the falling ratio partly
reflects length, not style alone.

unambiguous single tags; the remaining word-units are particles and
other function words, so no family taxonomy is asserted.

### Distinctive vocabulary by period (keyness, G2) ~

Keyness (Dunning's G2) measures how distinctively a root's
word-unit frequency in one revelation period differs from the
rest of the corpus. The top 15 roots by G2 are listed for
each of the four periods, by Cairo 1924 revelation order
(Nöldeke-Bell four-period classification). Periodization
varies across scholarly chronologies; treat these rankings as
Nuanced, not as a settled chronology.

● Leeds corpus v0.4.

ℹ How this is computed

●
G2 computed from per-period root counts in word-units
( data/roots-summary.json ) against period word-unit
totals ( data/numbers.json ), by
scripts/compute-association-stats.mjs .
~
on the period assignment itself (Cairo 1924 / Nöldeke-Bell).
Full root-frequency and keyness tables (CSV/JSON):
Export .

### How evenly roots are spread across the Qur'an ●

Frequency alone cannot tell whether a root recurs across the
whole text or clumps inside a few surahs telling one story.
Gries's Deviation of Proportions (normalized, DPnorm) measures
exactly that, for every root with at least 20 corpus-wide
occurrences: 0 means the root's occurrences track surah size as
closely as possible; 1 means total concentration in the
smallest surah.

Per-root detail (DP, DPnorm, Juilland's D, range, adjusted
frequency): open any root on the Roots page .

ℹ How this is computed

●
Computed by scripts/compute-dispersion.mjs over
the 114 surahs, weighted by word-unit count (not treated as
equal-sized). DP = 0.5·Σ|v_i − s_i|; DPnorm = DP / (1 −
min(s_i)), the corrected normalization from Lijffijt &
Gries (2012). Roots below 20 corpus-wide occurrences are
excluded from this ranking (though every root's own DP/DPnorm
still appears on its Roots page detail) since a rare root is
trivially maximally concentrated without that being
informative. Full per-root table (CSV/JSON):
Export .

===== How to use this site (https://divinediscourses.org/how-to-use) =====

## How to use Divine Discourses

This site is not Google. It is a workbench for studying the Qur'an the
way Dr. Khan taught. One surah at a time. As a coherent discourse.
With attention to language and structure.

## Four ways to start

Ask right here

Search

Go to a passage

Explore

Pick a surah you want to understand.
Type its name or number in the Ask box above —
Arabic script works too.
Examples: Fatihah, al-Asr, 103, 2,
الفاتحة .

Look up one verse.
Type the reference.
Examples: 1:1, 2:255, 103:1,
٢:٢٥٥ .

Investigate a word.
Type the English meaning or the Arabic root — separated letters
or joined script.
Examples: mercy, patience, r-h-m, s-b-r,
رحم .

Compare two ideas.
Open Compare and set two roots side by
side. Try r-h-m (mercy) against '-dh-b (punishment) to see how
the Qur'an balances the two.

## Three depth levels

Simple shows verse text, word-by-word meanings, and
translations. Use this to read.

Study adds word-by-word grammar (morphology) and root links —
and, on the Read, Dossier and Replay pages, the reading lenses card
and the discovery worksheet for your own structural reading. Use
this for close analysis.

Encyclopedic adds structural patterns and full
sources. Use this to verify.

Change depth with the gear icon, bottom right, or press
1 (Simple), 2 (Study), or 3
(Encyclopedic) on any page. Your selection is saved in your
browser. Every claim on the site carries a small verification pill —
see what the labels mean .

## The method Dr. Khan taught

A surah is one discourse, not a collection of verses. Read it whole.
Find the central claim. Trace the words that carry that claim back to
their roots. See how the structure of the surah serves its message.

The
Exercise on Surah al-Asr demonstrates
this method on the shortest meaningful surah. Start there if you have
ten minutes. The reading lenses card on Read, Dossier and Replay
(Study depth) then lets you apply this and two other published
coherence methods — the Farahi–Islahi ʿamūd questions and a ring
overlay — to any surah, in your own words.

## What the labels mean

Every factual claim on this site carries one of three small pills.
Hover or tap a pill to read its definition.

●

Verified — drawn from the Leeds Corpus or
another named primary source.

○

Pending — awaiting triangulation from a second
independent source. Treat as provisional.

~

Nuanced — the counting method varies across
sources. See the source detail for the specific approach used.

This site does not generate exegesis. Every interpretive claim is
sourced. The full method behind these labels — and the canonical
definition of each — is documented on
Validation .

## If you get stuck

Open the Exercise page. Watch the method work on al-Asr. Then come
back and try the same approach on a surah you choose.

You can reopen the welcome tour anytime from the "?" button on the
home page (bottom right, next to the
settings gear), or follow one of the guided
study paths step by step.

===== How the method works (https://divinediscourses.org/how-it-works) =====

## How It Works

Divine Discourses follows a coherence-based method for reading the Qur'an,
drawing on the work of Hamiduddin Farahi (1863–1930), Amin Ahsan
Islahi (1904–1997), and Dr. Irfan Ahmad Khan (1931–2018).

### The method

The coherence-based approach, developed by Hamiduddin Farahi and his
student Amin Ahsan Islahi, treats the Qur'an as a unified text with
internal structure. Each surah is read as a coherent whole with a
central theme, and verses are understood in relation to the surah's
structure and to parallel passages elsewhere in the text. This
approach contrasts with atomistic reading that treats each verse in
isolation.

Dr. Irfan Ahmad Khan (1931–2018) was a founding scholar of the
Association of Quranic Understanding and carried forward this
coherence-based method in his teaching and published works. His
Reflections on the Qur'an (Islamic Foundation UK, 2005)
demonstrates this approach on the first two chapters of the Qur'an,
and his An Exercise in Understanding the Qur'an (Association
of Quranic Understanding, 2013, ISBN 9781567447736) applies it
systematically across the last thirty surahs.

Khan emphasized that the believer's task is to engage the text
directly, not through an intermediary. He taught that every reader
builds their own personal relationship with the Qur'an, and that this
relationship requires patient attention to the text's own structure
and cross-references. Divine Discourses gathers tools that support this kind
of direct engagement, roots, words, patterns, frequency, and
structural markers, with provenance records on research claims so
readers can see exactly what was checked and trace sources independently.
The Read, Dossier and Replay pages render three such published
methods as a reading lenses card — scaffolding for your own
reading, never the site's interpretation.

### Three depth levels

Every page on this site can be viewed at one of three depth levels.
You choose your depth based on what you need in the moment.

Simple

?

The reading layer. Verse text, word-by-word meanings,
translations, and audio. No morphology tables, no annotations.
Use this when you want to read without distraction.

Study

?

The analytical layer. Adds word-by-word morphology, root links,
related verses, and chronological period distribution — including
the reading lenses card on Read, Dossier and Replay. Use this
when you want to understand how words work and how themes recur.

Encyclopedic

?

The reference layer. Adds structural pattern notes and full
provenance for every claim. Use this when you want to verify
sources or understand where the data comes from.

Change depth anytime using the gear icon in the bottom right, or
press 1 , 2 , or 3 on any page. Your
selection is saved in your browser, never sent anywhere. No
tracking, no cookies.

### Evidence status

Research claims distinguish source inspection, computational
reproduction, method dependence, and known limitations. The familiar
dot remains a compact summary and citation control; it is not a claim
that every dimension has been independently verified.

●
— Confirmed from a primary corpus or canonical edition. The source
is named and linked.

○
— Awaiting triangulation from a second independent source before
being marked Verified.

~
— The counting method or interpretation has known variation across
sources. See the source detail for the specific approach used.

The Validation page is the canonical
definition of these labels and of the process that assigns them. You
can use its prompts to triangulate any Pending claim against outside
tools and references of your choice, or to surface the nuance in any
Nuanced claim.

### Sources

Data on this site comes from named corpora, APIs, published scholarship, and primary-source references; provenance and licensing are documented on the Sources page.

Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 (Language Research
Group, University of Leeds, 2009–2017, GNU GPL) for word
morphology, root tagging, and grammatical analysis.
corpus.quran.com

Quranic Universal Library (Tarteel AI / Quran.com
Foundation, 2024) for structured verse data and corpus indexing.
qul.tarteel.ai

Quran.com Foundation Content API v4 (Quran.com
Foundation, 2025) for translations, recitations, and metadata.
api-docs.quran.foundation

Full citations for all sources, including access dates and version
numbers, are on the Sources page.

The research and tooling behind this site may use software
assistance, including language models, to locate candidate
sources and check work. Everything published is verified by a
person against the cited source; interpretations, translations,
and glosses come only from the named human scholarship cited.

### The text behind the numbers

Two limits of the data deserve plain statement.
○
First: the Arabic text rendered here (the Tanzil Uthmani text) and
the Leeds tokenization behind every count follow the reading of
Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim with the Kufan verse numbering — the reading used
in most printed muṣḥafs today. The Qur'an has other canonical
readings ( qirāʾāt ) that differ in places, so every count
on this site is relative to this one reading; none is a count of
"the Qur'an" independent of it.

Second: the Leeds corpus's version 0.4 is its most recent release,
and the project is no longer actively updated. Like any large
annotation effort it contains imperfections, and assigning a root
or lemma to a word — especially weak roots and hamza spellings —
involves editorial judgment by its annotators. When this site
marks a corpus-derived count Verified, that means the computation
from the cited corpus is faithful and reproducible; the count
inherits whatever imperfections the corpus itself carries.

### Where the numbers come from

None of the counts on this site are typed in. The scripts that
produce them ship in the repository alongside the corpus data, and
every figure quoted in a page's prose is bound to the generated
dataset, so a page cannot drift from the data behind it: an
automated check fails the build if it does. Run any generator
twice and the output is identical, which is what makes an
independent recomputation possible. The
Datasets page lists each dataset and
the script that builds it.

One boundary is worth naming, because counting can look like
claiming. The recurring-phrase index records that a sequence of
words repeats and where. Whether such repetition amounts to
formulaic composition in the oral-formulaic sense is a scholarly
question, argued at length by Bannister (2014, on
Sources ); the site counts the
recurrence and leaves the argument to the literature.

### How themes are built

Each theme on the Themes page begins with
a small set of triliteral roots whose core dictionary senses relate
to it. That grouping is an editorial choice, labeled Nuanced
wherever it appears. What follows is computed: the site counts
where those roots occur, ranks the passages in which the theme's
vocabulary clusters, and links them. A theme can live in verses
that use none of its words, and any of those words can appear
outside the theme, so a theme is a gateway into reading rather
than an index of where an idea is present.

### How this compares to other Qur'an tools

Many excellent Qur'an apps and websites exist, and this site links
to several of them. The differences below are matters of design
policy, stated so you can decide whether they matter for your own
study — not claims that other tools are wrong to choose otherwise.

Common elsewhere
Here

Built-in commentary telling you what a verse means

No commentary of the site's own. The site computes structure
and cites published scholarship; what a verse
means is left between you and the text. Khan's
readings appear only as verbatim transcriptions from his
published books, with citations.

An assistant that answers questions in its own words

A deterministic Ask box: pattern-matching that routes your
question to the right tool. The site never answers in its
own voice.

Counts and claims presented without provenance

Every research claim carries a badge — ● Verified, ○
Pending, ~ Nuanced — that decomposes into named evidence
dimensions you can check yourself on the
Validation page.

Accounts, sync, analytics, engagement mechanics

No accounts, no tracking, no streaks. Notes and preferences
stay in your browser; the only network requests fetch the
text, translations, and audio you ask for.

Verse-by-verse browsing as the primary frame

The surah as one discourse is the primary frame, following
the coherence-based approach described above — with
structural evidence (roots, recurring phrases, rhyme,
cross-references) gathered per surah in the
Dossier .

### A suggested first visit

If this is your first time using Divine Discourses, here is a walkthrough
that touches each major feature.

Open al-Fatihah 1:1 and read the
basmala in multiple translations at Simple depth.

Switch to Study depth (gear icon in bottom right) and reload the same
verse to see word-by-word morphology with root links.

Visit the Roots page and click any row to
see how that root distributes across the Meccan and Medinan periods.

Use Compare to overlay several roots at
once — try faith (a-m-n), works (ʿ-m-l), and righteousness (ṣ-l-ḥ)
together to see the verses where all three meet. Compare can also
set passages, or whole surahs, side by side on their corpus
fingerprints.

Visit Patterns to see grammatical shift
(iltifat) and recurring formulations (mutashabihat) at work in the
text.

When you have completed the first visit, try the
coherence-reading exercise on Surah al-Asr . This is the method this site honors, demonstrated live on the
shortest meaningful surah.

===== Guided study paths (https://divinediscourses.org/paths) =====

## Study paths

Guided walkthroughs that chain the site's tools into a method. Each
step links to a live page; nothing here adds interpretation — the
paths only order the evidence.

### Path 1 · Follow a root through the Qur'an

Take r-ḥ-m (mercy) from a single verse to its full corpus
distribution.

Read it in context:
al-Fatihah 1:1 — two of the
four words carry the root.

Open the root's profile:
r-ḥ-m on Roots — 339
occurrences, derived forms, Makki/Madani split, every verse
reference.

See what it travels with: the co-occurring roots section on the
same page — gh-f-r (forgiveness) is its most frequent verse-level
companion.

Compare passages where it clusters:
al-Fatihah vs the opening of Maryam
in Compare's Passages mode.

### Path 2 · Profile a surah before reading it

Build a structural picture of a surah from the data, then read it
with that frame.

On Navigate , open the Profile panel
for a surah (try 103, al-'Asr): verse count, distinct roots, top
roots, chronological period.

Check its length band against the era pattern on
Numbers (verse length by period).

Read it end to end on
Read at Study depth
(press 2 ) with word-by-word morphology on.

Test your structural reading in the
al-'Asr outline exercise .

### Path 3 · Trace a claim to its source

The site's core discipline: never take a number on trust —
including ours.

Pick a claim on Numbers , for example
the top-five root frequencies.

Click its badge (●): the popover shows the full Chicago-style
citation of the source.

Follow the source entry on Sources to
the primary corpus at corpus.quran.com and check one number
yourself.

Run a triangulation prompt from
Validation against an independent
tool, and see whether it converges on the same figure.

### Path 4 · Study a theme end to end

Move from a life theme to the passages where its vocabulary
clusters, and form your own reading of what they agree on.

Pick a gateway on Themes (try
Forgiveness ) and note its
root families — the gateway is lexical, a starting point rather
than an index.

Open two or three of its key passages on the Read page and read
each whole discourse around the verse, not just the verse
itself.

Use the theme card's "top two passages side by side" link to
see, in Compare, which roots the passages actually share.

Follow the theme's most frequent root into
Roots : where else does it cluster, and
in which period? Write down what the passages agree on and
where they differ.

### Path 5 · Test a Khan outline against the site's own computed signals

Propose your own structure, reveal Dr. Khan's published outline,
then see what the site's mechanical tools find — or don't find —
in the same surah.

Work through the
al-'Asr outline exercise :
propose your own verse-by-verse structure before revealing
Khan's.

Open the same surah's Dossier .
Its Structure section shows the site's own computed discursive
pivots and rhetorical features for this exact surah; its Rhyme
and Formulas sections show the verse-ending pattern and
recurring-phrase data. The mirror-structure (ring-composition)
test ran across the whole corpus and nothing held up in any
surah — so the Dossier says "no result" rather than showing
one; read the test itself on
Patterns . Not every
mechanical detector finds something in every surah, and an
empty section is a finding in its own right, not a gap.

Follow whichever signal caught your eye to its full method and
corpus-wide result on Patterns .

Return to Read at Study
depth and write in the discovery worksheet where Khan's outline
and the site's computed signals agree, diverge, or simply
don't overlap.

### Path 6 · Read one surah through three lenses

Take al-'Asr — three verses — through three published coherence
methods: Khan's transcribed outline, the Farahi–Islahi ʿamūd
questions, and a ring-structure overlay you mark yourself.
Unlike Paths 1–5, which each drive one tool, this path holds
one text still and varies the method (nazm reading in three
forms).

Work the
al-'Asr outline exercise :
propose your own verse-by-verse structure, then reveal Khan's
transcribed outline and compare.

Read al-'Asr on Read at
Study depth and open the ʿAmūd worksheet in the Reading lenses
card: answer the method questions in your own words — the site
transcribes no ʿamūd statement for any surah.

Open the same surah's Dossier ,
read its computed Structure signals, then switch the Reading
lenses card to the Ring overlay and mark your own candidate
members and centre — the site asserts no ring for any surah.

Still on the Dossier, ask where the three readings agree and
diverge: does your ring centre coincide with your ʿamūd? With
the pivot in Khan's outline? A method that finds nothing in a
surah is also a result.

Step checkmarks are saved in this browser only and are cleared by
the settings panel's "Clear preferences".

===== Glossary of terms used here (https://divinediscourses.org/glossary) =====

## Glossary

Specialist terms used across the site, with plain-language
definitions. Terms with a dotted underline on any page reveal their
definition on hover or tap.

Ayah آية

A verse of the Qur'an. The plural is ayat. The same word also
means "sign."

Basmala بسملة

The opening formula bismillah al-rahman al-rahim ("In the
name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful"). It
heads 113 of the 114 surahs and appears mid-surah once, at 27:30.

Betweenness centrality

How often a node lies on the shortest paths between other nodes in a co-occurrence network. A statistical position measure, strongly influenced by raw frequency; it does not indicate importance.

Buckwalter

A one-to-one Latin-character transliteration system for Arabic,
used by the Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus to encode the consonantal
and vowel structure of every word in machine-readable form.

Corpus

The machine-readable text this site computes from — here, the Leeds
Quranic Arabic Corpus, a word-by-word analysis of the Qur'an. A corpus
is something you count over, not an interpretation: every figure on
this site is a count made against it.

Deterministic

Producing the same output for the same input, every time, by
following fixed rules. The Ask box is deterministic:
pattern-matching routes your question to a tool, and nothing
composes an answer on the site's behalf.

Dice coefficient

The Dice coefficient: the overlap between two words' sets of verses, from 0 (never together) to 1 (always together).

Discourse

As used on this site: a surah read as one connected address
(khitab) from speaker to hearer — a single speech with a
beginning, development, and close — rather than a loose
collection of verses. The site's name, "Divine Discourses,"
carries Khan's translation of khitab.

Eigenvector centrality

Eigenvector centrality: a node scores high when its neighbors also score high, meaning proximity to network hubs. A statistical position measure; it does not indicate importance.

Evidence dimensions

The separately recorded aspects of a research claim's support
on this site: what source was checked, whether the computation
was reproduced, what the result depends on, and its known
limits. A claim's badge summarizes these; the
Validation page decomposes them.

Hapax

From hapax legomenon (Greek: "said once"). A word or form
occurring exactly once in a corpus. The Qur'an has roughly 12,000
surface-form hapax legomena and roughly 395 root-level hapax.

Iltifat التفات

Grammatical shift, especially person or tense, treated by
classical Arabic rhetoricians as a deliberate rhetorical device
rather than a textual irregularity.

Juz جزء

One of the 30 roughly equal parts the Qur'an is traditionally
divided into (plural ajzāʾ ; also called para ),
so that reading one each day completes the Qur'an in a month. Unlike
a surah, a juz can begin and end in the middle of a chapter. The
boundaries are a reading convention, not part of the revealed text.
Browse them on Navigate .

Keyness

A score (Dunning's G2) for how distinctively a word belongs to one section of the text compared with the rest. High keyness means the word's frequency there is statistically unusual, not that the word is important.

Khitab خطاب

Direct address from speaker to hearer. In the
Farahi-Islahi-Mir-Khan tradition that shapes this site, khitab is
treated as the proper unit of Qur'anic reading. The site's name,
"Divine Discourses," renders God's khitab to the hearer.

Lemma

The dictionary or canonical form of a word. In Arabic morphology,
lemmas are derived from triliteral roots according to fixed
patterns.

LLR (log-likelihood ratio)

Log-likelihood ratio (Dunning's G2): a score for how surprising it is that two words share verses as often as they do, given how often each occurs overall. Higher means stronger evidence the pairing is not chance. It measures distribution, not meaning.

Morphology

The word-form analysis of Arabic: root, stem pattern, prefixes,
suffixes, tense, mood, person, number, and inflection. The Leeds
Quranic Arabic Corpus provides this analysis for every word in the
Qur'an.

Mutashabihat متشابهات

Phrases or formulations that recur across the Qur'an with small
variations. The classical science of tracking these parallels is a
subfield of 'ulum al-Qur'an .

Nazm نظم

Arabic for "coherence" or "structural order." A method of Qur'anic
exegesis that reads each surah as a unified composition with
deliberate thematic structure, developed by Farahi, Islahi, Mir,
and Khan.

Nuanced

A claim that is defensible but depends on a specific counting
rule, classification scheme, or interpretive choice. Both the
headline figure and the underlying ambiguity are presented.

Pending

A claim awaiting triangulation. Useful as a working figure but not
yet verified against primary sources.

Period distribution

How a word or root's occurrences distribute across the Meccan and
Medinan revelation periods, based on a chosen chronology such as
the Cairo 1924 edition or Nöldeke-Schwally.

PMI (pointwise mutual information)

Pointwise mutual information: how much more often two words appear together than chance would predict. Rare, tightly paired words score high; very frequent words score low even when they co-occur often.

Provenance

Where a figure or claim comes from: the named source, edition,
and method it can be traced to. On this site every research
claim carries its provenance — a citation you can follow and a
badge stating how far it has been checked.

Inclusio

A bracketing device where a unit's opening and closing share
vocabulary or a phrase, framing what sits between them. A
narrower, more specific pattern than ring composition
generally. This site tests it mechanically, over computed
sections, never as a scholar's reading. See
Patterns .

Ring composition

A structure in which a text's opening and closing mirror each
other around a centre (A-B-C-B-A), so the middle carries the
weight. Documented in the Qur'an by Cuypers, Farrin and others.
This site names the phenomenon but asserts no specific ring
outline for any surah: doing so means transcribing a published,
page-cited analysis, not computing one. See
Patterns for the two
mechanical proxies the site did test (one over individual root
positions, one over computed sections), and both null results.

Root

The three-letter (occasionally four-letter) consonantal skeleton
from which Arabic words are derived. Every noun and verb in the
Qur'an fits a root into fixed morphological patterns; the same
root can carry a family of related meanings.

Surah سورة

A chapter of the Qur'an. There are 114, varying in length from 3
verses to 286.

Surface form

A distinct written form of a word as it actually appears in the
text, before it is reduced to its dictionary form. The same
lemma can appear as several
surface forms (singular, plural, with attached prefixes). The
Qur'an has 18,993 distinct surface forms across its 77,429
word-units .

Tafaseer

Plural of tafsir.

Tafsir تفسير

Qur'anic exegesis or commentary. A scholarly genre going back to
the earliest generations of Islam.

Token (word-unit)

One word as the Leeds corpus lists it; this site calls it a
word-unit in plain language. The corpus follows
the written words of the Uthmani text, so bismi ("in the
name of") is one word-unit, and the Qur'an has 77,429 of them.
The corpus also splits each word into morphological segments
( bi + ism , 130,030 segments in all); this site
takes a word's root, lemma and part of speech from its stem
segment and does not count segments. Counts of nouns, verbs, and
verse length on Numbers are measured in
word-units.

Triangulate

To cross-check a claim against two or more independent sources.
Agreement across sources moves a claim from Pending to Verified;
disagreement keeps it Nuanced with the disagreement recorded. See
Validation for the prompts.

TTR (type-token ratio)

Type-token ratio: distinct word forms divided by total words, a measure of vocabulary variety. Smaller samples score higher mechanically, so the trend matters more than the absolute values.

Verified

A claim on this site backed by direct corpus data, primary text,
or peer-reviewed scholarship. The strongest confidence label.

Word-unit

This site's plain-language name for a corpus
token : one written word of the
Uthmani text as the Leeds corpus lists it. Used in place of
"word" so a count is not mistaken for dictionary words or for
morphological segments.

Fāṣila

The word or syllable a verse ends on. When the same ending recurs across
consecutive verses it produces the rhyme or assonance pattern (fawāṣil,
plural) scholars read structure from.

Qasam

An oath opening: a surah or passage that begins by swearing on something
(time, the sun, the fig tree) before making its claim. Surahs al-'Asr,
al-Shams, and al-Tin open this way.

Parallelism

Balanced clause or phrase structures, where successive units
echo each other's grammar or meaning. Concentric parallelism,
where the echo runs from a text's edges toward its centre, is
one specific case. See Ring composition .

Fawātiḥ

The "opening letters" (also called al-muqatta'at, "the disjointed letters"):
one to five Arabic letters that open 29 surahs, in 14 distinct combinations,
before the surah's first sentence. Their meaning has never been settled in
the classical tradition.

Oral-formulaic

A framework from the study of oral literature, applied to the Qur'an by
Bannister (2014), that reads recurring phrases as evidence of formulaic
composition. This site counts recurrence mechanically; whether that
recurrence is oral-formulaic in this technical sense is the scholarly
argument, not something the count settles.

Formula

A sequence of three to five consecutive words that recurs somewhere else in
the Qur'an, counted by root sequence or by surface form on the Formulas
page. What is counted is recurrence; whether a formula is formulaic in the
technical oral-formulaic sense is a separate scholarly question.

Benjamini-Hochberg correction

A statistical correction applied when many hypotheses are tested at once
(every surah, or every root pair), controlling the false discovery rate
(FDR): the expected share of "significant" results that are actually false
positives. Used throughout this site's corpus-wide tests instead of judging
each result alone.

Null distribution

The range of results a statistic would produce under a random or shuffled
version of the data, used as the yardstick a real result is judged against.
A result counts as significant when it falls where the null distribution
says chance rarely lands.

Nöldeke-Bell

A four-period chronological classification of the surahs
(three Meccan periods plus Medinan), descended from Theodor
Nöldeke and Friedrich Schwally's source-critical scholarship as
adapted by Richard Bell. This site pairs it with the Cairo 1924
edition's revelation order. See Watt's Bell's Introduction to
the Qur'an on Sources .

Revelation order

The sequence the surahs are traditionally held to have been revealed in,
distinct from their fixed position in the mushaf (the standard printed
Qur'an). This site follows the Egyptian Standard (Cairo 1924) revelation
order, a convention rather than a documented historical record.

Uthmani

The standard Arabic script and verse divisions used in nearly all printed
and digital copies of the Qur'an today, following the consonantal skeleton
fixed under the caliph Uthman. The Arabic text on this site is the Tanzil
Uthmani edition.

Normalized frequency

An occurrence count divided by the size of the text it is drawn from (here,
per 1,000 tokens), so counts from different-sized samples, such as the
Meccan and Medinan periods, can be compared directly.

Tokenization

Splitting text into countable units (tokens). The Leeds corpus
lists the Qur'an's written words and splits each into
morphological segments ( bismi into bi +
ism ). This site counts the words, 77,429 of them, not
the segments.

Discursive pivot

A verse mechanically flagged for opening with a temporal
particle (like idh or idha ) while sharing
vocabulary with what precedes it, a candidate marker of where a
passage turns. Detected by pattern matching, not by a scholar's
reading. See Patterns .

Centrality

A family of statistical measures of a node's position in a network, such as
this site's root co-occurrence graph. This site reports degree, betweenness,
and eigenvector centrality; none of them indicate a root's importance, only
its structural position.

Tadabbur

Reflective, contemplative study of the Qur'an, read as a connected discourse
rather than isolated verses. The term names the reading approach behind
Islahi's Tadabbur-i Qur'an and this site's discovery-worksheet exercises.

Formulaic density

The share of a verse's or surah's words that belong to a recurring formula,
operationalizing the central quantity in Bannister's (2014) computerized
oral-formulaic study. This site tests whether a surah's density is higher
than a length-matched resampling of corpus verses would predict, correcting
for the fact that short surahs mechanically show noisier density than long
ones.

Dispersion

How evenly a root's occurrences are spread across the 114 surahs, as distinct
from raw frequency. This site reports Gries's Deviation of Proportions (DP,
DPnorm) and Juilland's D side by side, since the two can disagree and the
literature has no single preferred measure.

Juilland's D

An older lexical-dispersion measure (Juilland & Chang-Rodriguez 1964), on
a 0-1 scale where 1 is perfectly even. It classically assumes comparably-sized
corpus parts; this site's 114 surahs range from 3 to 286 verses, so it is
reported for comparability with the literature, not as the preferred measure.

ʿAmūd عمود

In the Farahi–Islahi coherence school, the central theme — literally
'pillar' — around which a whole surah is organized, with each part of the
surah read in relation to it. Described in Mustansir Mir's 1986 study of
Islahi's nazm method. This site transcribes no ʿamūd statement for any
surah; its ʿamūd reading lens offers method questions only, for the
reader's own answer.

Sirah سيرة

The biographical literature on the Prophet's life, against which a surah's
conventional revelation placement is often read. This site registers Ibn Isḥāq's
sirah ( Guillaume's 1955
translation ) as a reference work for the history reading lens but
transcribes nothing from it and asserts nothing from that literature: the
lens shows only the conventional chronology and hands the sirah questions
to the reader.

Asbāb al-nuzūl أسباب النزول

The classical genre recording the occasions on which particular verses are
reported to have been revealed. This site registers al-Wāḥidī's
Asbāb al-Nuzūl (Guezzou's
2008 translation) and Rippin's 1988
study of the genre as reference works for the history lens but
reproduces none of their reports; where the lens asks about a surah's
moment, the answer is the reader's own, built from sources they consult
themselves.

Reading lens

A published coherence method rendered as UI scaffolding on the Read, Dossier
and Replay pages: Khan's transcribed outlines, the Farahi–Islahi ʿamūd
worksheet, or a ring-structure overlay. A lens frames the reader's own study;
it never asserts what a verse means, and the reader's answers never carry a
verification badge. Distinct from the homepage daily card's rotating data
'lens', which is a corpus statistic.

This glossary is also available inline throughout the site. Technical
terms are marked with a dotted underline and reveal their definition
on hover or tap. Categories: Method (nazm, khitab, tafsir,
mutashabihat, iltifat, triangulate). Structure (surah, ayah, basmala).
Data (root, morphology, lemma, token / word-unit, corpus, hapax,
Buckwalter, period distribution). Claim labels (Verified, Nuanced,
Pending).

===== Core Qur'an vocabulary: 475 lemmas, 80% of lemmatized words (https://divinediscourses.org/vocabulary) =====

## Core vocabulary

A small set of words carries most of the Qur'an. Of its
77,429 word-units in the Leeds corpus,
74,122 carry a lemma (a dictionary headword); the other
3,307 are standalone pronouns and the disconnected letters
that open 29 surahs. The 475 most frequent lemmas account for
80% of those 74,122.
●

### How many lemmas cover how much

Share of lemmatized word-units Lemmas needed Word-units they cover

50% 61 37,108

70% 239 51,931

80% 475 59,316

90% 1,119 66,712

Counted from the Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 lemma field,
most frequent first. Coverage by lemma counts every form of a
word as the same word, so knowing a lemma is not the same as
recognizing each of its forms in context.

word-by-word English for this form at its first occurrence,
fetched when you ask for it and not stored on this site.
~
A word can mean something different elsewhere; follow the verse
link to see it in context.

attached prefix or suffix), its part of speech, its root, how often
it occurs, the running share of lemmatized word-units, and the
first verse where that form appears. A lemma the corpus tags more
than one way shows its most frequent tag.

===== Search this site (https://divinediscourses.org/search) =====

## Search this site

Every page section, glossary term, cited source, and theme, in
one index. For a verse, a surah name, or a root, the
Ask box is faster; everything else lands here.

Search needs JavaScript : the index is
matched in your browser, nothing is sent anywhere. Without
scripts, the same ground is covered by the
Glossary , the
Themes index, the
Sources list, and the site map in
the footer of every page.

Search terms

Search

Try:
iltifat ·
hapax ·
chronology ·
verse length
