===== Sources, cited in full (https://divinediscourses.org/sources) =====

## Sources

Every dataset, translation, scholarly work, and tool that Divine Discourses
draws on, with license and verification status.

Entries follow the Chicago Manual of Style, bibliography form. Where a
detail (edition, place, or year) could not be confirmed against the
work itself, it is omitted rather than guessed. Entries whose data or
tooling the site actually consumes carry a clickable ● badge that
opens the machine-readable registry record; purely bibliographic
entries are verified by the citation itself and carry no dot. Translations rendered
on the Read page are served through the alquran.cloud API; the print
editions cited are the originals of those renderings.

### Primary text

Tanzil Project. Tanzil Quran Text , Uthmani script, Version 1.1. 2007–.
https://tanzil.net/ .
Creative Commons Attribution 3.0, verbatim copies only. Bundled with
this site unchanged, with Tanzil's notice.
●

King Fahd Complex for the Printing of the Holy Qur'an.
Mushaf al-Madinah . Madinah: King Fahd Complex.

### Morphology and lexicography

Dukes, Kais. The Quranic Arabic Corpus , version 0.4. Leeds:
Language Research Group, University of Leeds, 2009–2017.
https://corpus.quran.com/ . GNU GPL. Morphological annotation of all 77,429 word-units of
the Qur'an; bundled in this site as per-surah JSON in
data/morphology/ and aggregated in
data/roots-summary.json . Version 0.4 is the corpus's
most recent release and the project is no longer actively
updated; its root and lemma assignments involve annotator
judgment (notably weak roots and hamza spellings), and counts
derived from it inherit any annotation imperfections it carries.
●

Lane, Edward William. An Arabic-English Lexicon . 8 vols.
London: Williams and Norgate, 1863–1893. Public domain.

Penrice, John.
A Dictionary and Glossary of the Kor-ân . London: Henry S.
King, 1873. Public domain.

Hava, J. G.
Arabic-English Dictionary for the Use of Students . Beirut:
Catholic Press, 1899.

Wehr, Hans. A Dictionary of Modern Written Arabic . Edited
by J Milton Cowan. 4th ed. Wiesbaden: Otto Harrassowitz, 1979.

Farahi, Hamiduddin. Mufradat al-Qur'an .
●

### Patterns and cross-references

Tarteel AI and Quran.com Foundation. "Mutashabihat Dataset," 2024.
Quranic Universal Library . Approximately 5,277 entries.
https://qul.tarteel.ai/ .

Quranic Universal Library . Approximately 4,001 pairs.

### Coherence-based reading

Farahi, Hamiduddin. Mufradat al-Qur'an ;

Coherence in the Qur'ān: A Study of Iṣlāḥī's Concept of Naẓm in

9780892590650. Independent scholarly corroboration that Islahi's
method, and the coherence-based reading school generally,
descends from Farahi's Mufradat and Niẓām — the second source
that moved the Farahi entry above from Pending to Verified.

Coverage page as one of the
obvious starting points for a page-cited ring outline; this site
asserts no outline from this book, only the mechanical
block-structure test on Patterns .

Ghamidi, Javed Ahmad.
https://www.ghamidi.org/ .

### Khan's works and lineage

Dr. Irfan Ahmad Khan (1931–2018) directed the Association of Quranic
Understanding and is the principal influence behind this site. His two
English-language works are listed below.

Khan, Irfan Ahmad.
Reflections on the Qur'an: Understanding Surahs al-Fatihah and
al-Baqarah . Markfield, Leicestershire: Islamic Foundation, 2005. The first
volume of Khan's English-language tafsir, covering the opening two
surahs.
Kube / Islamic Foundation UK .

Khan, Irfan Ahmad.
An Exercise in Understanding the Qur'an: An Outline Study of the
Last Thirty Divine Discourses (Surah 85 to Surah 114) . Foreword by Mustansir Mir. Chicago: Association of Quranic
Understanding, 2013. 213 pp. ISBN 9781567447736. Khan's
outline-structure methodology applied to the final thirty surahs.
Available through AQU and major Islamic bookstores.

Khan, Irfan Ahmad.
An Introduction to Understanding the Qur'an with Examples .
Compiled by Tanveer Azmat. Chicago: Association for Qur'anic
Understanding, 2011. Two methodological chapters followed by six
worked surahs (96, 103, 107, 108, 109, 112) — each with the Arabic
text, a word-by-word gloss, an outline structure, and an
interpretation. Distributed by the AQU at
quranicunderstanding.com . The outline exercises for surahs 96, 107, 108, 109, and 112 and
the word-by-word English glosses for all six surahs (the Meaning
column on the reading page) on this site are transcribed from this
volume.

bibliography; it does not mean the Divine Discourses site uses it as a data
source.

Shah, Mustafa, and Muhammad Abdel Haleem, eds.
The Oxford Handbook of Qur'anic Studies . Oxford: Oxford
University Press, 2020.

International Qur'anic Studies Association (IQSA).
https://iqsaweb.org/ .

### Rhetoric and stylistics

Abdel Haleem, Muhammad. "Grammatical Shift for Rhetorical Purposes:
Iltifāt and Related Features in the Qur'ān."
Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 55,
no. 3 (1992): 407–32.

Abdel Haleem, Muhammad.
Understanding the Qur'an: Themes and Style . London: I. B.
Tauris, 1999.

Neuwirth, Angelika.
Studien zur Komposition der mekkanischen Suren . Berlin:
Walter de Gruyter, 1981.

Cuypers, Michel.
The Composition of the Qur'an: Rhetorical Analysis .
Translated by Jerry Ryan. London: Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

Bannister, Andrew G.
An Oral-Formulaic Study of the Qur'an . Lanham, MD:
Lexington Books, 2014. ISBN 9780739183571. Cited as context for
this site's recurring-phrase index: the index records the
mechanical fact of recurrence; whether recurrence constitutes
formulaic composition is the scholarly question this book
argues.

Serves the word-by-word meanings shown beneath each verse on the
Read page. Fetched per passage at runtime and cached only in the
reader's browser; no word-translation text is bundled in this
repository, and copyright remains with the translation's rights
holders. A word-by-word gloss is a translator's choice of one
English word for one Arabic word, so it is labeled Nuanced
wherever it renders.

Islamic Network. Recitation audio CDN , per-ayah MP3,
multiple reciters.
https://cdn.islamic.network . Serves the recitation audio on the Read and Replay pages; the
reciter is chosen from the microphone button beside each verse.
●

Islamic Network. English translation audio edition ,
en.walk , verse by verse.
https://cdn.islamic.network . The English leg of Listen mode on the Read page, played after
each verse's Arabic. Three things are worth separating here, and
the third is why this entry is not marked Verified.
What the edition is : alquran.cloud's own edition
registry reports en.walk as “Ibrahim Walk”, language
English, recorded verse by verse;
scripts/check-audio-editions.mjs read that from the
API on 16 September 2026, and the name above is taken from that
response rather than from anywhere else.
Whether it plays : the same run found the CDN
serving it from the 192 kbps directory, after 128 and 64 had both
refused — which is why the player probes bitrates at runtime
instead of assuming one. The check found three Arabic reciters had
moved the same way.
What he reads : two primary sources agree. The
same registry describes a companion edition,
en.misharyrashidalafasyenglishtranslationsaheehibrahimwalk ,
as “Mishary Rashid Alafasy with Saheeh International translation
(Ibrahim Walk)”, and everyayah.com, a separate site that
also hosts per-ayah recitation audio, files his recording under a directory it names
Sahih_Intnl_Ibrahim_Walk_192kbps — both read on 16
September 2026. So the recording reads Saheeh International, the
translation this site shows by default. Not yet established is
that the CDN's file is that same recording rather than another
encode or take: its clip for 1:1 is 57,867 bytes against
everyayah.com's 171,910 — a size difference this large is itself
reason to doubt the two sites serve the same recording. Until one listening check settles that, the
Read page does not pair the audio with the text automatically.
Under what license : neither the registry nor the
CDN states who holds this recording or on what terms, so this
entry states neither, and stays Pending until one of them does.
○

Islamic Network. Translation audio editions in six further
languages , verse by verse.
https://cdn.islamic.network . Listen mode offers these as translation voices beside English:
ur.khan (Urdu, Shamshad Ali Khan),
fr.leclerc (French, Youssouf Leclerc),
ru.kuliev-audio (Russian, “Elmir Kuliev by
1MuslimApp”), zh.chinese (Chinese, no reader named),
kk.khalifahaltai-audio (Kazakh, Khalifah Altai) and
uz.sodik-audio (Uzbek, Muhammad Sodik Muhammad
Yusuf). What each edition is : the names and
languages above are the ones alquran.cloud's edition registry
gives, read by scripts/check-audio-editions.mjs on 26
September 2026. Whether it plays : the same run
found the CDN serving each one across early, middle and final
clips of the Qur'an. The registry lists four more non-Arabic
audio editions that this site does not offer, because none can be
played verse by verse: Persian and Turkish are registered as whole
translations rather than per verse, a Burmese edition is one file
per surah, and a second Russian edition is registered but served
at no bitrate. The registry lists no Bengali audio edition.
What each one reads : not established. A
recording may follow a different translation from the written one
on the page, so the Read page never pairs them. Under what
license : neither the registry nor the CDN states who
holds these recordings or on what terms, so this entry states
neither, and stays Pending until one of them does.

### Citation badge component

Every statistic on this site carries one of three claim badges:

●
Verified — confirmed from the primary source cited.
Where the badge is attached to a statistic, clicking it opens the
full citation (this example opens the Leeds corpus citation). On
this Sources page the citation is the entry itself.

○
Pending — sourced but awaiting a second independent
confirmation.

~
Nuanced — defensible but dependent on a specific
counting rule, classification scheme, or interpretive choice; use
with the linked note, which states the dependency.

The badge component is implemented in
assets/cite-badge.js (plain vanilla JS, no dependencies).
Add
<script src="assets/cite-badge.js"></script>
to any page and badges with data-source-ids attributes
will show click-to-expand citation popovers sourced from
data/sources.json .

### Editorial policy

Polemic sources are not used. The "scientific miracles" genre is
referenced for context, not as evidence.

Anonymous video or blog content is not cited.

The site treats Khan as its principal influence without placing him
in any single school.

===== How each claim is validated (https://divinediscourses.org/validation) =====

Evidence before confidence

## Validation methods

A single “verified” label can hide important differences. This site
records whether a source was inspected, whether a computation was
reproduced, whether the result depends on a corpus or classification,
and what its known limits are. These dimensions show what was checked
without claiming more certainty than the evidence supports.

Source check Was the cited artifact itself inspected?

Reproduction Can the result be rerun from named inputs and code?

Dependency Would another corpus, counting rule, or chronology change it?

Limits What does this evidence not establish?

## How we verify: worked examples

Each example is joined to a canonical claim record. Open a record to
inspect its stable ID, derivation, and limitations; click its dot to
inspect the bibliographic source records.

### ● Verified · top five roots

a-l-h (God, 2,851), q-w-l (say, 1,722), k-w-n (be, 1,390), r-b-b
(Lord, 980), a-m-n (believe, 879).

Source trace. Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus, Kais
Dukes 2009–2017, GPL-licensed. Dictionary interface at
corpus.quran.com . Full top-10 with per-root citations on
Numbers and
Roots . One primary source; independent
triangulation possible via any Qur'anic concordance.

### ● Verified · Farahi's Mufradat and Niẓām

Hamiduddin Farahi, Mufradat al-Qur'an and
Niẓām al-Qur'an . Foundational to the coherence-based
reading school.

Source trace. Primary: Farahi's own
Mufradat al-Qur'an and Niẓām al-Qur'an .
Independent secondary corroboration: Mustansir Mir,
Coherence in the Qur'an: A Study of Islahi's Concept of Nazm
in Tadabbur-i Qur'an (Indianapolis: American Trust
Publications, 1986, ISBN 9780892590650) — a scholarly monograph
devoted to showing that Islahi's nazm method, and by extension
the coherence-based reading school, descends directly from
Farahi's Mufradat and Niẓām. Two independent sources agree; full
citations on Sources .

### ~ Nuanced · y-w-m (day)

Root y-w-m occurs 405 times under the Leeds corpus's root
annotation. Claims of 365 or 475 use different selections of
surface and compound forms; they are not results reproduced here.

Why it stays Nuanced. The 405 total is recomputed
from the cited Leeds root annotations. The often-repeated 365 and
475 totals use other, usually unstated selection rules; no inspected
source or reproducible procedure for them is presently in this
site's evidence record. They are mentioned only to show why the
unit and inclusion rule must be declared, not as verified
alternatives. Detail on
Numbers .

### ● Verified · mercy travels with forgiveness

The root r-ḥ-m (mercy) co-occurs with gh-f-r (forgiveness) in 91
verses — its most frequent verse-mate by a wide margin (its
next-closest partner shares 37).

Source trace. Counted from this site's bundled
verse-level co-occurrence tables ( data/cooccurrence/ ),
derived from the Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 — recomputable
from the data we ship. r-ḥ-m and gh-f-r share 91 verses; r-ḥ-m's
next-closest partner shares 37, and the pairing is also the top
result from gh-f-r's side (91), so it is not an artefact of one
root's raw frequency. The count is descriptive: it shows the two
ideas are voiced together, not what any verse means. Open either
root on Roots to see its co-occurrence
network.

### ● Verified · hapax legomena

12,004 surface forms (out of 18,993 unique forms) occur exactly
once in the Qur'an. 395 roots (out of 1,642 ) occur exactly once.

Source trace. Computed directly from the Leeds
Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 word-form and root tables, which are
bundled in this site's own data/morphology/ files —
so the claim is recomputable by anyone, from the data this site
ships, without trusting us. Note what recomputability proves:
that the figure is faithfully derived from the cited corpus.
Its correctness inherits the corpus's own annotation accuracy
(see the corpus note on
How it works ). Published on
Numbers at Study depth.

### ● Verified · a two-source claim

547 roots appear only in Meccan surahs; 198 appear only in
Medinan surahs.

Why two sources. This claim combines the Leeds
corpus (which roots occur in which surahs) with the Cairo 1924
edition's Meccan/Medinan classification. The badge cites both;
click it to see the pair. A nuance rides along: a handful of
surahs are classified differently in other traditions, so the
boundary counts can shift by a few under other schemes — the
claim on Numbers carries that note
beside it.

### ~ Nuanced · "this world" and "the hereafter"

A popular claim holds that "this world" ( al-dunyā ) and
"the hereafter" ( al-ākhira ) each occur exactly 115 times.
At the root level the counts are not equal: d-n-w occurs 133 times
and a-kh-r 250 times. The 115/115 parity holds only for particular
surface forms under one counting rule.

Why it stays Nuanced. The often-repeated "115
each" figure counts specific surface forms (such as the definite
al-dunyā and al-ākhira ) under one selection rule.
At the level this site computes — the triliteral root — the counts
differ: d-n-w appears 133 times and a-kh-r 250 times (a-kh-r also
carries senses like "last" and "other"), both verified from the
Leeds corpus and recomputable from
data/roots-summary.json . We report the honest root
numbers and note that a matched count depends entirely on which
forms one chooses to count — the same caution the y-w-m example
makes. This site does not endorse numerical-parity claims it
cannot reproduce.

## Triangulation prompts

These prompts are optional discovery aids for locating sources or
competing formulations. Their output must never become site content,
a citation, or an authority. Inspect the primary artifact yourself,
record its locator, and independently reproduce any computation.

### Prompt 1: Verify a root count

Using only verifiable academic sources (Quranic Arabic Corpus at corpus.quran.com, Tanzil text, Lane's Lexicon, Penrice's Dictionary of the Koran, or peer-reviewed Qur'anic studies journals), how many times does the triliteral root [INSERT ROOT, e.g., r-ḥ-m] appear in the Qur'an? Distinguish (a) root occurrences, (b) surface form occurrences if relevant, (c) any counting variation between sources. Cite each source. Do not estimate; if uncertain, say so.

Copy prompt

### Prompt 2: Verify a numerical claim

The following claim about the Qur'an circulates widely: [INSERT CLAIM]. Investigate with academic rigor. (1) What counting rule does it use? (2) What do alternative counting rules yield? (3) What is the academic position, citing peer-reviewed sources? (4) Is the claim broadly accepted, or are there nuances? Provide direct citations.

Copy prompt

### Prompt 3: Verify Islahi-school content

In Amin Ahsan Islahi's Tadabbur-i-Qur'an (Lahore: Faran Foundation), what is the stated 'amud (central axis) of Surah [INSERT NUMBER AND NAME]? Provide the Urdu phrasing if available, the English translation if accessible (e.g., Shehzad Saleem at al-Mawrid), and the volume and page reference.

Copy prompt

### Prompt 4: Verify chronology

For Surah [INSERT NUMBER], what revelation order is assigned by each of: (1) Cairo 1924, (2) Nöldeke-Schwally 1909, (3) Bell 1937, (4) Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2012? List each ordering's position number and qualifications. Cite the source for each.

Copy prompt

### Prompt 5: Verify iltifat

Does Qur'an [INSERT VERSE] contain an instance of iltifat (grammatical shift in person, number, addressee, tense, case, or structure)? If yes, describe and cite Abdel Haleem's 1992 BSOAS article or other peer-reviewed sources. If borderline, state that.

Copy prompt

Workflow. Use an assistant, catalog, or search engine
only to locate candidate material. Then inspect the cited artifact,
record precisely what it supports, reproduce computations from pinned
inputs, and preserve disagreements. Assistant agreement is never a
review stage and never changes a claim's evidence status.

===== Datasets, documented for reuse (https://divinediscourses.org/datasets) =====

## Datasets — take the data, check the work

Every number on this site is computed from data that ships with the
site. This page documents each dataset for reuse: what it contains,
the script that generates it, its license, and a direct download.

Regeneration is deterministic: run any listed script twice and the
output is byte-identical. The full pipeline and every generator
live in the
public repository
(directory datasets are easiest to grab there — clone or use the
per-directory links below). Licensing in one line: data derived
from the Leeds corpus is GPL ; site code is
MIT . Details in
NOTICE.md .

### Corpus foundation

#### data/morphology/{1..114}.json

Word-by-word morphology for all 77,429 word-units: per verse, an
array of words, each
{w, ar, root, lemma, pos, gloss} (word index,
Uthmani surface form, Buckwalter root, Buckwalter lemma,
part-of-speech tag; the per-word-unit gloss field is empty — the
word glosses that ship live separately in
data/gloss/ , six surahs from Khan 2011).
●

Derived from Leeds Quranic Arabic Corpus v0.4 · GPL ·
generator scripts/build-leeds.js ·
sample (surah 1) ·
full directory

counts, per-chronology-period counts, first/last occurrence, and
surface-form inventories.

Root-pair association statistics per root: the top 25 partners

formulas and thresholds live once in

full directory

Precomputed, deterministic radial layouts for each root's
association ego network (static x/y coordinates, no browser
layout), plus the top-40-roots-by-114-surahs density matrix
behind the Numbers page heatmap.
●

GPL · generator compute-network-layout.mjs ·
sample (r-ḥ-m) ·
heatmap ·
full directory

#### data/centrality/{root}.json × 1,642

Network centrality per root over the association graph: degree
(raw and normalized), weighted degree, betweenness (Brandes),
and eigenvector centrality (power iteration), each with its
rank out of all 1,642 nodes. Algorithms and the graph
definition live in centrality/methods.json .

GPL · generator compute-centrality.mjs ·
sample (r-ḥ-m) ·

full directory

### Structure, sound, and phrase recurrence

#### data/formulas-root.json · data/formulas-surface.json

Every 3-, 4-, or 5-word-unit sequence recurring 2+ times corpus-wide, with
all verse locations — root-sequence and surface-form streams
(each catches phrases the other cannot). Browsable on
Formulas .
●

GPL · generator build-formulas.mjs ·
root stream ·
surface stream

#### data/formulaic-density.json

Per-verse and per-surah share of words covered by a recurring
formula (Bannister's oral-formulaic density), tested per
surah against a length-matched resampling null, pooled into
one Benjamini-Hochberg correction across both streams. Method
and citations in the file's own _method /
_hypothesis fields. Browsable on
Formulas and per-surah on
Dossier .
●

GPL · generator build-formulaic-density.mjs ·
download

#### data/rhyme/{1..114}.json · data/rhyme-summary.json

Verse-ending (fāṣila) analysis per surah: each verse's final
word reduced to an approximate pausal form, rhyme families under
a fine and a coarse ending key, shift points, and refrains. An
orthographic proxy, not a phonological transcription — the
method note inside each file states the limits.
~

GPL · generator build-rhyme-map.mjs ·
sample (surah 91) ·
summary ·
full directory

#### data/rhetorical-features.json · data/discursive-pivots.json · data/symmetry-test.json

Direct-address formula locations and muqaṭṭaʿāt letters;
verse-initial temporal-marker boundaries with lexical
continuity; and a significance-tested (and honestly null)
rare-root symmetry check — including its full statistical
method.
●

GPL · generators
build-rhetorical-features.mjs ,

build-symmetry-test.mjs ·
rhetorical-features ·

symmetry-test

### Wanted: surah outlines to transcribe

Dr. Khan's 2013 volume publishes sectional outlines for surahs
85 to 114
● . The transcribed ones power the outline exercises; the rest
are this project's open work queue. Claiming one means
transcribing from the book under the review checklist in
CONTRIBUTING.md , or submitting your own structural hypothesis for it, which
needs no book at all. The reading lenses card on the Read page
surfaces this queue per surah: an untranscribed surah in the
85–114 range says so in place.

Loading the outline queue…

### Wanted: ring and structural analyses

Ring composition, where a surah's opening and closing mirror
each other around a centre, is documented in the scholarly
literature. This site names the phenomenon and asserts no ring
outline for any surah, because a real one has to be
transcribed from a published, page-cited analysis, never
computed. Inventing verse ranges under a scholar's name would
misattribute work they did not do, so the count below is zero
and stays zero until someone brings a citation. The ring lens
on Read, Dossier and Replay is this queue's reader-side
complement — a blank overlay for your own candidate ring, never
a transcribed analysis.

Claiming one means naming the scholar, the volume and the page,
and giving the verse ranges exactly as published. Cuypers,
Farrin ●
and Islahi ●
are the obvious starting points. The
Patterns page carries
the one narrow mechanical proxy the site did test corpus-wide,
and its null result, which says nothing either way about that
literature.

Loading the structural queue…

## Export: download the numbers

Eighteen precomputed tables, each as CSV and JSON: root
frequencies, dispersion and counts by surah, lemma frequencies,
root-pair association statistics, per-surah stats, verse lengths
and recitation durations,
formulas and formulaic density, centrality, rhyme summary,
fawātiḥ, direct address, discursive pivots, computed structure
and its tests, and theme-surah density. Every field is
documented in the schema and data dictionary below. For the complete raw pipeline (morphology,
per-root files, and every other dataset this site ships), see
Datasets .

Generated deterministically by
scripts/build-exports.mjs , which reads
data/roots-summary.json ,
data/numbers.json ,
data/chronology.json ,
data/surah-profiles.json ,
data/surah-names.json ,
data/morphology/ , and the association statistics from
data/association/*.json (written by
scripts/compute-association-stats.mjs ). Run either
script twice and the output is byte-identical. Both scripts and
the full pipeline live in the
public repository .

NOTICE.md
for the complete notice. Chronology-derived fields (period,
revelation order) use the Cairo 1924 revelation order, whose
periodization varies across scholarly chronologies. The export
code itself is MIT licensed, like the rest of the site.

### Downloads

#### Root frequencies ● ~

All 1,642 roots: raw count, overall normalized frequency (per
1,000 word-units), and per-period count and normalized frequency
across the four revelation periods (Cairo 1924 / Nöldeke-Bell).

CSV
JSON
1,642 rows

#### Root dispersion ●

All 1,642 roots: how evenly each is spread across the 114
surahs, weighted by surah size — Gries's DP, its Lijffijt &
Gries normalization, Juilland's D, the count of surahs the root
occurs in, and a dispersion-adjusted frequency. Four measures
side by side rather than one, because the literature disagrees
about which is best. Same figures as the
Numbers table and the
Roots root-detail panel.

CSV
JSON
1,642 rows

#### Roots by surah ●

Every root in every surah it appears in: the count, and the rate per
1,000 of that surah's tokens, one row per root per surah. The full
matrix behind the per-surah counts on the
Roots detail panel, ready for a spreadsheet
pivot or a heat map. A missing row means the root does not occur
in that surah.

CSV
JSON
17,496 rows

#### Lemma frequencies ●

Every lemma (dictionary headword) in the corpus: its count, part of
speech, root if it has one, most common written form, how many
distinct forms it takes, and how many verses and surahs it occurs
in. The word-level companion to the root tables, and the list a
vocabulary course would start from.

CSV
JSON
4,832 rows

#### Direct address to the believers ●

Every verse containing yā ayyuhā lladhīna āmanū (&ldquo;O
you who believe&rdquo;), matched on lemmas so inflected forms
count. The list behind the vocative count on
Patterns . Other vocatives are not
included.

CSV
JSON
89 rows

#### Verse durations ~

Every verse with its length in word-units and how many seconds
its recitation lasts in each recording Read
plays, one column per reciter. Measured from the audio files'
headers; no audio is included. A duration describes one
recording's performance, not the text. Summarized as pace on
Numbers .

CSV
JSON
6,236 rows

#### Association pairs ●

Root-pair association statistics (shared verses, LLR, PMI,
Dice): the union of every pair appearing in any root's
top-25-by-LLR partner list. Same formulas and thresholds as
the Roots statistical-associations
panel; see the schema for the exact counting rule.

CSV
JSON
5,211 rows

#### Per-surah stats ● ~

All 114 surahs: verse/word-unit/root counts, vocabulary-diversity
ratios, noun/verb percentage, and Cairo 1924 revelation order
and period.

CSV
JSON
114 rows

#### Verse lengths ●

Every verse in the corpus with its length in word-units and revelation
period.

CSV
JSON
6,236 rows

#### Formulas ●

Every recurring 3-5 word sequence in the Qur'an, root-view and
surface-view combined, with its first occurrence. Same counts
as Formulas ; full occurrence lists are
in data/formulas-root.json and
data/formulas-surface.json .

CSV
JSON
18,408 rows

#### Centrality ~

All 1,642 roots: degree, weighted degree, betweenness, and
eigenvector centrality over the root co-occurrence graph, each
with its rank. Same figures as the
root detail centrality panel.

CSV
JSON
1,642 rows

#### Rhyme summary ●

All 114 surahs: verse-ending rhyme family count, dominant key
and share, shift count, top refrain, and mean run length. Same
figures as the Patterns rhyme
panel.

CSV
JSON
114 rows

#### Fawatih ●

The 29 surahs opening with isolated letters (al-muqatta'at)
and which of the 14 distinct combinations each uses. No
meaning is asserted for the letters.

CSV
JSON
29 rows

#### Discursive pivots ~

137 verses mechanically flagged for opening with a temporal
particle while sharing a root with the previous verse, a
candidate marker of where a passage turns, not a scholar's
reading.

CSV
JSON
137 rows

#### Computed structure ~

Mechanically segmented sections for all 114 surahs (417
sections total), a changepoint model over lexical cohesion,
never attributed to any named scholar. See the
Dossier "Computed structure" panel.

CSV
JSON
417 rows

#### Structure tests ~

Four block-level mirror-symmetry tests over the computed
sections, one row per surah. 0 of 345 candidates reached
significance after correction; see
Patterns .

CSV
JSON
114 rows

#### Theme-surah density ~

Sparse theme-by-surah matrix: for each surah, the themes whose
root-family vocabulary clusters most densely in it (theme-root
word-units per 1,000 surah word-units). See Themes .

CSV
JSON
252 rows

#### Formulaic density ~

All 114 surahs: mean share of words covered by a recurring
phrase (root and surface streams), tested against a
length-matched resampling null, with a Benjamini-Hochberg
survivor flag. Same figures as Formulas .

CSV
JSON
114 rows

### Schema and data dictionary

Every field, its unit, its counting rule, and its Verified/Nuanced
status is documented in both a machine-readable schema and a
prose data dictionary:

schema.json (machine-readable)
DATA-DICTIONARY.md (prose)

### Everything at once, pinned to a version

One archive holds all eighteen tables in both formats, the schema,
the data dictionary, and a citation file, so a download never
travels without its provenance. The archive is named by release
version and built deterministically: citing
v1.3.0 names these exact bytes, and
a new release adds a new archive rather than replacing this
one. For toolchains that read standard packaging, the same
tables are described as a
Frictionless Data package
and as
Croissant JSON-LD .

divinediscourses-data-v1.3.0.tar.gz (all tables + schema + citation)

Earlier releases stay downloadable, because a published citation
points at the bytes it was written against:
v1.0.0 .

===== Changelog: every correction logged (https://divinediscourses.org/changelog) =====

## Changelog

Every correction and material change to Divine Discourses since launch.
Logged here as a record of accountability. Site maintainers commit to
logging future corrections in the same place.

Historical entries keep the vocabulary of their day — for example,
the middle depth tier appears as "Scholar" in entries written
before it was renamed "Study".

### 2026

#### September

Core vocabulary, and a corrected definition.
Core vocabulary lists the 475 lemmas
that account for 80% of the Qur'an's 74,122 lemmatized word-units
(Leeds corpus), most frequent first, each with its root, count and
first occurrence. A practice mode shows one word at a time and,
on request, the Quran.com word-by-word English for it at that
verse; progress stays in your browser. Also corrected: the
glossary said a word-unit is a piece smaller than a written word
(bismi as two). It is one written word, as the Leeds corpus lists
them; the 77,429 figure counts written words.
§

A page for every juz, and for every common root.
Each of the 30 juz has a page at /juz/<number>
(for example /juz/1 ): where it starts and
ends, its verses, word-units and mushaf pages, the surahs it
spans, and how long it takes with each reciter. Each of the 411
roots that occurs 20 or more times has a page at
/root/<key> (for example
/root/qwl ): its count and rank, lemmas,
written forms, the surahs where it concentrates and the roots it
keeps company with. Surah pages now print cleanly. Two fixes:
juz 4 now starts at 3:93, as the Tanzil metadata marks it, not
3:92; and three part-of-speech labels on Roots (exceptive,
explanation, exhortation particles) now match the corpus's tags.
§

A reference page for every surah. Each of the 114
surahs now has a plain page at /surah/<number>
(for example /surah/36 ): verse and
word-unit counts, classification and revelation order, juz and
mushaf pages, listening time for each reciter, most frequent
roots, the computed sections, themes whose vocabulary clusters
there, recurring phrases, verse endings, and the full Arabic text
from Tanzil with its notice. Everything is read from the site's
own data files and readable with JavaScript off, so search and
answer engines can find and cite it. Navigate
links to all of them. Also: the sitemap's dates now follow each
page's real changes, and one uncited appeal to "academic
literature" on Numbers is gone.
§

Version 1.3.0: four more tables to download, and how long a
recitation takes.
Export adds roots by surah (every
root's count and rate in every surah it appears in, 17,496 rows),
lemma frequencies (all 4,832 lemmas with part of speech,
root, most common form, and spread across verses and surahs),
direct address (the 89 verses with &ldquo;O you who
believe&rdquo;), and verse durations (how long each verse's
recitation lasts in each recording Read plays). The first three were
already computed for the Roots and Patterns pages but could not be
downloaded; each is checked against files computed separately.
Durations are measured from the audio files' own headers, without
downloading the audio. Numbers
now shows each reciter's listening time and pace, overall and by
period, and Read's listening options show how long the passage takes
with the chosen reciter. A duration describes a recording, not the
text. The v1.3.0 archive holds all eighteen tables; earlier archives
are unchanged.
§

The Arabic text now ships with the site. Read and
Compare take the Arabic from Tanzil's own Uthmani file (Version
1.1), bundled unchanged with Tanzil's notice, and fetch only the
translations. If the translation service is down, the Arabic still
shows, with a note. Before this, the Arabic came from alquran.cloud,
whose copy matched Tanzil's current file in 2,619 of 6,236 verses:
the differences are small marks (the small meem written for some
tanwin, the form of some hamzas, a small yeh), not words. Readers
will see those marks change. Also corrected: the site described
Tanzil's license as CC BY-ND 3.0; Tanzil's file states Creative
Commons Attribution 3.0, verbatim copies only, notice retained.
§

The cross-reference dataset and every feature built on it are
removed. The verse-to-verse cross-references bundled since
July 2026 came from a corpus whose compiler published no license, and
whose repository later became unreachable; no license could be
obtained. Rather than keep an unlicensed redistribution, the data,
the Related-verses panel on Read, the browser on Patterns, and the
connectivity figure on Navigate, Compare and each dossier are gone,
and the two registry entries that described them are retired.
Nothing derived from that corpus remains in data/ or the
exports. Separately: three of the five reciters had been silent on
every page (served at 64 kbps while each player asked for 128); the
bitrate now lives on each reciter and the audit checks it. Listen
mode reaches any passage on Read, and Replay shares its engine.
§

Three sirah and occasions-of-revelation reference works
are now registered, and the Mishkat entry records that its
upstream repository went dark.
The history lens's sirah worksheet had said the site registered
no sirah or asbab al-nuzul source. It now names three — al-Wāḥidī's
Asbāb al-Nuzūl in Guezzou's translation, Ibn Isḥāq's
sirah in Guillaume's translation, and Rippin's 1988 study of
the genre — on the Sources
page, and the lens, the glossary entries for
sirah and
asbāb al-nuzūl , and the
maintainer guide now say so.
Registering is not transcribing: no occasion
report is reproduced for any surah, the worksheet stays blank,
and the site still asserts nothing about any surah's
historical moment. Separately, the GitHub repository the Mishkat
cross-reference corpus was copied from stopped answering; its
entry now records that with the date, keeps the date the copy was
taken, and drops the dead link rather than guessing at an
archive — the bundled data and its license-pending standing are
unchanged.
§

#### August

Plain language everywhere a reader meets a count.
A site-wide copy pass replaced the corpus term token
with the site's own plain name,
word-unit , in all reader-facing
copy — homepage daily card, Read, Navigate, Dossier, and the deep
analytics pages — with every figure unchanged. Statistical
results now lead with plain phrasing (what held up, what chance
predicts) and keep the exact statistics in parentheses.
Part-of-speech tags on the Read page render as full names (Noun,
Proper noun) instead of raw codes. The inline glossary learned
plural forms (tokens, word-units, lemmas) — its word-boundary
rule had silently never matched a plural — and gained an entry
for corpus .
No number, counting rule, or method statement
changed; method notes and this changelog's own history keep
token where precision requires it. One sentence also
became more accurate: the daily card's vocabulary-variety line
had presented the distinct-root count as a count of word-units;
it now states the ratio as what it is, distinct roots over
word-units. §

A history lens: when a surah sits in the conventional
chronology, and who it names.
The reading lenses card gained a fourth lens. It shows the
Egyptian Standard revelation order and Nöldeke–Bell period the
site already carried for all 114 surahs — labeled as the
convention it is, with the manuscript-evidence caveat cited —
and, for the first time on this site, the proper names each
surah uses, computed from the corpus's proper-noun tags.
Names carry no Arabic root, so every root-keyed dataset has
always been blind to them; a new generated index makes them
countable.
The sirah questions beneath those panels are
blank scaffolding: no sirah or occasions-of-revelation source
is registered here, and the site asserts nothing about any
surah's historical moment — the reader's answers stay in
the reader's browser. Romanized name labels are editorial
working labels, checked against the computed index in both
directions; counts measure distribution, not meaning, and a
name's absence is never a story's absence.
§

Reading lenses: three published coherence methods as
scaffolding.
The Read, Dossier and Replay pages gained a reading lenses card
at Study depth: Khan's transcribed sectional outlines where
they exist (six surahs), the Farahi–Islahi ʿamūd method as
site-authored questions for the reader's own answers, and a
blank ring overlay in the Cuypers/Farrin tradition. A guided
path, Read one surah through three lenses, walks al-'Asr
through all three, and the homepage now leads with that first
exercise.
The card asserts no structure and fills in
no answer: what is and isn't transcribed is stated on the
card itself, a build-time check holds the advertised coverage
to the transcription registry in both directions, and the
reader's answers stay in the reader's browser, exportable
and clearable from the card, never carrying a verification
badge.
§

The citation-link checker stopped mistaking GitHub for a dead
link.
Six links this site makes to its own files on GitHub — the
licence, the contribution guide, the notice file among
them — began reporting broken. Every one was present; an
unauthenticated automated request had simply been declined.
A link to a file in this repository is
now checked by reading the file, not by asking GitHub for
it — which also means a pull request that deletes one of
these files is now caught on that pull request, rather
than only after the deletion reaches the published site.
§

The root-density heatmap is 41% lighter, and shows
the same numbers.
Each of its 4,560 cells carried its own hidden label so a
mouse hover could show the value. Those labels were 4,560
of the page's 11,225 elements — the next heaviest page on
the site is under 2,800 in total. One label now serves the
whole chart, built from the cell you are pointing at.
The hover text is unchanged, checked
cell by cell in both column orders against the data file
the chart is drawn from. Nothing moved for keyboard
readers: the cells have never been focusable, and the
values have always also been in the “View as table (by
root)” panel below the chart, which is unchanged.
§

Six long pages now open with a list of their own
sections.
validation.html runs about eighteen screens on a phone and
offered no map of itself; sources, numbers, about, coverage
and patterns are all long enough to want one. How It Works
has had such a list since it was written, and this is that
same list applied to the pages that needed it.
The list is generated from the headings
already in each page, so it cannot drift from them, and it
is in the markup rather than built in the browser, so it
works with scripts off. A heading that already had an
address keeps it — nine on How It Works are linked from
other pages and none of them moved. Entries for sections
your depth level hides are hidden with them.
§

The root-dispersion table is downloadable from the
Export page.
It has been published since the measure shipped — in the
schema, the data dictionary, the citable archive and the
machine-readable dataset descriptions — but the Export page
offered thirteen download cards under a line promising
fourteen, and dispersion was the missing one. Its card is
now there, with the same 1,642 rows the archive carries.
Everything about a published table is
generated from one schema except its download card, which is
written by hand; that is how a table could be complete
everywhere a machine looks and absent where a reader looks.
A new check now holds the page, its stated row counts, its
table-count prose and the tables themselves against that
schema, and cross-checks every table against the data it is
derived from.
§

Ten pages stopped downloading a 126 KB lookup table
they barely used.
The table tells the page which words in its prose are Qur'anic
roots, so they can be tapped for a definition. It listed all
1,944 roots on every page that carried it; between them those
pages mention 25. Each page now receives only the entries its
own text can match — 5,560 bytes across all of them, against
128,998 before — and the three pages that mention no root at
all no longer load the feature.
Nothing a reader sees changed: every root
and verse reference wraps exactly as it did, verified by
comparing the rendered markup of all 30 references on the
affected pages before and after, byte for byte.
§

The coverage dashboard was under-reporting how many
sources are reachable from a badge.
It said 29 of 31, and with JavaScript off it said 25 of 31.
The registry had grown to 36 sources, 34 of them reachable,
and the measurement behind those figures had not been re-run
since. The two that remain unreachable are cited as further
reading only and are named on the page.
The generator that produces this report had
no staleness check, which is how a figure on the page whose
subject is honest accounting went two releases out of date. It
has one now, and it compares the measured content while
ignoring the date stamp, so it cannot pass merely because the
file was written today.
§

A shared reading link now shows the translations its
sender chose.
The ?t= parameter added last week only worked for
someone who had never set a translation preference of their own:
for everyone else the saved preference silently replaced the
link's, and the address bar was then rewritten to match, so
passing the link on lost the sender's choice a second time.
Compare had a matching fault -- opening a saved passage
comparison fetched the site's two default translations rather
than the reader's, and changing translations afterwards did
nothing until a full reload -- and its per-translation credit
line was printing the surah's name where the translator's should
have been, which also left right-to-left and non-Latin scripts
without their correct direction and typeface. A translation
retired from the registry can no longer get stuck in a saved
selection, uncountable and impossible to untick.
The regression tests for all of this ran in a
fresh browser profile, the one state where a saved preference
cannot contradict a link, which is why they passed over the bug.
They now start from a reader who has already chosen.
§

Version 1.2.0, and the data archive a citation names
can no longer change under it.
The download page told readers that citing
v1.1.0 named those exact bytes and that a new
release would add a new archive rather than replace the old
one. Neither was true. The version stayed at 1.1.0 while the
table set grew from four to fourteen, and the staleness check
compared the archive against the current tables — so
it kept demanding that the released bytes be overwritten. The
archive published as v1.1.0 was rewritten five times and ended
up holding ten tables it never published.
The genuinely released v1.1.0 bytes are restored from the
release commit, today's fourteen tables are published as
v1.2.0 alongside it, and every archive's SHA-256 is now
recorded in data/exports/RELEASES.json . The build
refuses to rewrite a published archive and tells you to bump
the version instead.
Also corrected: the download pages said
"four" and "twelve" tables where there are fourteen, and the
enumeration omitted dispersion and formulaic density.
§

Choosing translations no longer means scrolling five screens of checkboxes.
The old "N selected" button opened a search-less list of
every edition grouped by language, and every tap reloaded
the whole passage immediately -- ticking three boxes meant
three reloads. It now opens a searchable dialog (by
translator, language, or edition id), your current
selection sorts to a "Selected" group at the top, and every
change applies once, on confirm. The button itself now
names the translators you picked instead of just counting
them. Read 's address bar carries the
selection too ( ?t= ), so a shared link shows
the translations its sender actually saw. The
Compare page's passage view rendered
only the first saved translation and dropped the rest
silently; it now renders every one, each with its own
translator credit and correct script. The gear panel
(every page) gets a Translations row so the setting is no
longer Read-only.
§

18,408 recurring phrases now answer a harder question: how much of a surah are they?
The Formulas index already listed
every phrase that recurs somewhere in the Qur'an; it never
said what share of a given surah's words those phrases
actually cover, which is the central quantity in
Bannister's (2014) computerised oral-formulaic study. Every
surah now gets that number for both the root and surface
streams, tested against 10,000 length-matched resamples of
the whole corpus rather than eyeballed: 46 of 228
candidates (114 surahs x 2 streams) come back higher than
chance predicts after a joint Benjamini-Hochberg
correction. Surah 64 (At-Taghabun) tops the root-stream
ranking at 55.6% of its words, the worked example on
Validation ; the nine shortest,
most distinctive Meccan surahs (96, 100-112 and others)
sit at exactly 0%. New panel on every
Dossier page and a corpus-wide
ranking on Formulas; a 13th table on
Export .
§

A root's frequency was never the whole story; now its spread is measured too.
Every root already carried a raw count, but two roots with
the same count can look completely different: one recurring
across the whole text, the other clustered inside a
handful of surahs telling one story. Root
detail now reports a new dispersion panel for all 1,642
roots: Gries's Deviation of Proportions (DP, DPnorm,
corrected per Lijffijt & Gries 2012), Juilland's D, the
plain surah count, and a dispersion-adjusted frequency,
rather than picking one measure as authoritative, since the
literature does not agree which is best. j-h-m (Hellfire)
is the worked example on Validation :
it occurs in 18 of 114 surahs, moderate by plain range, but
those 18 are disproportionately short Meccan surahs, so its
normalized DP is 0.7989, near the top of the ranking.
Numbers gets a most/least evenly
spread ranking; Export gets a
fourteenth table; three new sources (Gries 2008, its 2012
correction, and Juilland & Chang-Rodriguez 1964) are
cited throughout.
§

Six sources got an id, and eleven numbers got a claim record.
Islahi, Farrin, Nöldeke and Schwally, Watt, Mustansir Mir's
1983 dissertation, and Sadeghi and Goudarzi were all
already cited in prose on Sources ,
but carried no machine-readable id, so no badge could ever
resolve to them; Farrin in particular had no citation
anywhere at all despite being named twice as a starting
point for ring-composition scholarship. All six now have a
full entry in data/sources.json . Separately,
eleven numbers this site had been showing for months
without a provenance record, the 89 direct-address verses,
the 29/14 fawatih count, both structural null results
(3,067 and 345 candidates, zero survivors either way), a
monorhyme surah, one root's association scores and network
centrality, the discursive-pivot count, an export's row
count, vocabulary variety by period, and the 18,408
recurring phrases, now each have a
claim record with its sources,
its reproduction method, and its limitations spelled out.
A new coverage measurement found that six sources,
including two load-bearing ones, khan-introduction-2011
and bannister-2014, were reachable from no badge anywhere
on the site; bannister-2014 is now cited on
Formulas . The Khan outline queue's
headline number turned out to conflate two different
books: of the six "transcribed" outlines in surahs 85-114,
only one is actually from the 2013 volume the queue is
named after, so 29 of 30 remain wanted from that book
specifically, not 24. Also fixed: a malformed prefilled
issue-link title on Coverage, and a hardcoded source count
in check-citation.mjs that would have quietly
stopped matching reality the next time a source was added.
§

Eight more download tables, and Compare stopped
front-loading 368KB nobody asked for. The public
Export page carried four tables since
its first release; it now carries twelve. The new ones
republish, as CSV and JSON with the same schema and data
dictionary as the rest, exactly what Formulas, the root
detail centrality panel, Patterns' rhyme ranking, the
fawatih count, discursive pivots, the computed-structure
panel, and the theme density behind Themes already show in
the browser, so any of it can be recomputed or reused
without scraping a page. Separately, Compare fetched its 368KB root list on
every visit, whether or not a reader ever searched for a
root; it now fetches that file on first use (typing into a
root field, following a deep link, or clicking one of the
example pairs) and not before. A blank visit to Compare no
longer downloads it at all.
§

The root you clicked is the root you get.
On Read , every word in the
word-by-word table links to its root, and opening one
showed a panel of frequencies, first and last occurrence
and derived forms under a green Verified marker. For most
roots that panel was wrong. The lookup compared the
corpus's Buckwalter spelling against an index keyed by
transliteration, case-insensitively, and Buckwalter uses
capitals for the emphatic consonants: lowercasing them
erased the difference. Only 683 of 1,642 roots resolved
correctly. 205 opened a different root altogether, so
r-ḥ-m, the root of mercy, rendered the figures for
d-r-h-m, the root of the coin; 754 more matched nothing
and produced a bare "Root data not available". All 1,642
now resolve, because the page already contained the
correct mapping a few hundred lines above the fault. Two
new guards keep it that way: a checker that holds the six
root datasets to one another and to the page's own
transliteration map, and a browser test that clicks a
root and reads the panel it opens.
§

Type a word, get somewhere. The Ask box
used to invite concepts like "mercy" and then refuse
them: an ampersand made it answer "not recognized", and
words that name both a chapter and an idea (light,
pilgrimage, repentance) silently opened the chapter and
buried the idea. Now a reference goes straight to the
text ("2:255", "surah 36", "juz 5", "para 3", all 30 juz
landing on the verse they begin at), an unambiguous name
still jumps to its surah, and a genuinely ambiguous word
opens Search showing the chapter,
the theme and the root side by side so you choose. The
index behind that page grew to hold all 114 surahs, all
30 juz and every root that carries an English gloss, and
both halves of the matcher now connect "creation" to the
gloss "to create". Nothing dead-ends: a query with a
letter in it always lands somewhere that can help, and
Roots offers a site-wide search
when its filter finds nothing. A 42-query acceptance
corpus runs the real router and the real matcher on every
release.
§

Seventeen languages to read alongside the
Arabic. Read gained Turkish,
Bosnian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Persian,
German, Hindi and Swahili, joining the seven already
there. Each script gets typography that respects it:
bundled faces for Devanagari and Bengali, a Naskh setting
for Persian rather than the Nastaliq used for Urdu, and
wider line height for the CJK scripts. Every edition id
was confirmed against the live translation service before
it shipped, and an edition whose translator the service
does not name ships unnamed rather than borrowing a name
from somewhere else. The weekly check now also proves
that every edition offered has a label and that no label
points at an edition that is gone.
§

Guided paths that follow you across the site, and
a site that works offline. Each of the five
learning paths now carries a time
estimate and hands every step a ribbon on the tool page
it sends you to, so you can see "step 2 of 4" and move
forward or back without returning to the list. Progress
stays in the same single preference key as everything
else. Separately, the site now caches its shell the first
time you visit, so a later visit with no connection still
renders and says so plainly instead of failing. An
accessibility pass fixed a hidden form field that keyboard
users could still land on, added missing control labels,
and turned heading structure, form labelling and colour
contrast into checks that run on every push rather than a
paragraph promising they were considered.
§

A search page, a contribution page, and see-also
links. Search matches the
whole site in your browser against a committed index;
nothing you type leaves the page, because there is no
server to send it to. Contribute
gathers what a submission is, the worksheet that produces
one, the issue templates it fits, and a standing call for
translators. Coverage now names
the specific surah outlines that are wanted, each with a
prefilled issue link. Surah dossiers and theme cards grew
a see-also panel built by joining the theme index against
the root co-occurrence data, so related material is one
click away rather than a search away.
§

Readable by machines, not just by people.
Every page now carries structured data describing what it
is: the datasets on Export , the
defined terms in the Glossary , the
typed works on Sources , the
learning paths, the breadcrumb trail. Two plain-text
summaries at /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt give an AI
reader the same tour a person gets. The changelog became
data, so this page and a new Atom feed at /feed.xml are
generated from one registry and can never disagree. The
data exports gained a Frictionless data package, a
Croissant description, a reproducible archive and a
per-dataset licence label, including the one whose licence
is still pending.
§

Cite this page. The site could tell you
where its evidence came from but gave you no way to cite
it back. Every page footer now offers a citation in
Chicago, APA and BibTeX form with the canonical URL, the
version and the access date; the repository carries a
CITATION.cff; and one version file feeds all of them, with
a check that fails the build if any of them drift apart.
Each claim on Validation gained
a permanent anchor you can link to, and the method page
was broken into sections that can be cited individually.
The glossary became a single registry, so the terms in the
page and the terms the tooltips use can no longer diverge.
A code of conduct, a security policy and a correction form
on every page arrived at the same time.
§

A card per surah, an app that installs, and a
citation you can check. Sharing a surah or a
theme now unfurls with its own image — the surah's Arabic
name, verse count, and place in the revelation order, or
the theme's root families — instead of one image for the
whole site. Installing the site as an app gets three
shortcuts (Read a passage, Today's discourse, Browse
surahs) and a proper preview. Behind both: a new check
that confirms the word-by-word translator credit against
what the Quran.com endpoint actually serves, so that
citation stops resting on documentation and starts
resting on a response — it runs with the weekly citation
and edition checks, and stays quiet unless something
really changed.
§

One share button that always shares the right
thing. The floating share button now follows what
is on screen: a theme card on
Themes or a rendered
Dossier hands out that entity's
link-preview page, so a pasted link unfurls with its own
title and description. The 33 per-card Share chips on
Themes are gone and the Embed chip moved to a study-only
row, so a theme card at Simple depth shows no buttons at
all. On Read , each verse's
reference (103:1) is now itself a link to that verse —
right-click or long-press to copy — and the native share
sheet carries a readable label like "al-'Asr 103:1-3".
Citation popovers gain a "Copy citation" action, the
share button now also exists on
Coverage and
Export , and the link-preview
pages and site card were regenerated with fuller
metadata.
§

Word meanings in the text itself. The
Read page now shows a published
word-by-word English meaning beneath every verse, at every
depth: the written word above its meaning, reading right to
left like the verse. The meanings are fetched per passage
from the Quran.com Foundation Content API and cached in your
browser only, the same way the verse translations already
worked; nothing is machine translated, no word-translation
text is stored in this repository, and the rights holders
are credited on Sources . The word
table's outbound dictionary links, which used to stand in
for a meaning the site could not show, are replaced by a
single link in the caption.
§

Pages about the text, not about the site. The
home page's explanations of how the site verifies itself, its
three depth levels, and its purpose all lived in full on the
method pages already, so they now live there only; what is
left is a reading path from the hero to today's discourse.
Provenance follows the same principle: a source badge already
opens its full citation and license, so each card now shows
the badge and a short source name, with the method sentences
one click away in a collapsed note. On a phone the Numbers
page sheds 250px of repeated citation prose.
§

Simplicity with avenues for depth. The
depth system now does what it promises. A saved depth
applies before first paint (no more flash of Simple), the
Simple/Study/Encyclopedic control sits at the top of
Roots ,
Numbers ,
Patterns ,
Dossier , and
Themes with its 1/2/3 keys
documented beside it, and the heaviest pages were
reorganized so Simple is genuinely simple: duplicate
renderings of the same data were merged behind view
toggles, statistical ledgers moved to Encyclopedic (their
cautions stay visible), and the self-study kit on Themes
is stated once instead of 33 times. Nobody arrives to
nothing: Roots and Dossier open on labeled examples,
Words gained one-tap example searches, Compare's examples
show at every depth, and the Ask box now also lives on
Read and
How to use . Statistical
labels lead with plain language ("Strength of evidence
(LLR)") with glossary definitions one tap away, Prev and
Next continue across surah boundaries, analysis pages end
with contextual "Explore further" links, and on phones
the floating buttons no longer overlap and navigation
targets keep a full tap size.
§

Open-source audit. A full-repository audit
ahead of open-sourcing. Licensing: the LICENSE file now
states that MIT covers the site's own code while bundled
data and fonts keep their own licenses, and NOTICE.md now
lists every computed dataset, including the five analytics
directories added in the releases below. Fixes: a stray
word removed from the Numbers
day-month-year card, the offline cache now includes the
chart helper script it had missed, chart tooltips can be
dismissed with Escape from every chart, period labels on
Navigate now match the rest of
the site, a theme distribution strip that could hang on
"Computing" now reports failure, and the recurring-word
highlights on Read announce
themselves to screen readers as actionable.
§

Coverage dashboard and network centrality.
A new Coverage page reports,
from direct measurement of the bundled data files: how many
of the 77,429 word-tokens carry a root, lemma, and
part-of-speech tag; that no verified root-gloss source
exists (0 of 1,642); cross-reference coverage (110 of 114
surahs, naming the four not covered); documented
counting-rule sensitivities; and a source registry that
records unstated fields as unstated rather than inferring
them. Root pages gained a "Network position" panel (degree,
weighted degree, betweenness, eigenvector centrality, each
with its rank), labeled with the caution that centrality
tracks raw frequency and does not indicate thematic,
exegetical, or theological importance.
§

Chart layer for the association statistics.
A zero-dependency SVG helper now draws: an association
network on each Roots detail page
(positions precomputed offline, nothing laid out in the
browser), a frequency-across-periods line, a verse-length
histogram, and a root-density heatmap of the top 40 roots
across all 114 surahs on Numbers ,
with a canonical/revelation-order toggle. Every chart
carries a table fallback and the caution that position,
distance, and color indicate statistical measures only.
§

Association statistics and public data downloads.
Root pages gained a "Statistical associations" table (shared
verses, log-likelihood ratio, pointwise mutual information,
Dice) over verse-level co-occurrence; Numbers gained normalized
frequencies per 1,000 tokens and a keyness-by-period card.
A new Export page offers four
tables as CSV and JSON with a machine-readable schema and a
prose data dictionary.
